commands.name: bg
commands.summary: let a stopped job carry on in the background.
commands.details:
exec hello   ... Ctrl+Z     stopped
  bg                          [1] hello &   (it runs, the prompt stays)

Default: the newest stopped job. It gets SIGCONT; the shell does not
wait for it (`fg` would).
commands.uses: process_get_table (core/process), scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), signal_send (core/signal), atoi, ui.

commands.name: exec
commands.summary: load an ELF program and run it.
commands.details:
exec hello       run it in the FOREGROUND: the shell waits until the
                   program ends; Ctrl+C ends it, Ctrl+Z stops it (a
                   stopped job: `jobs`, `fg`, `bg`)
  exec hello &     run it in the BACKGROUND: the prompt comes back at
                   once (stop it later with `kill <pid>`)

Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the shell, which is running this command. We
pass it on the way a terminal does: the foreground program is ended.
The kill goes through process_kill(), so kill_guard still decides.
commands.uses: elf_load_and_run (core/elf), process_get_by_pid / process_kill (core/process), sys_sleep_interruptible (syscalls/sleep), arg_next (lib/args), ui_* (ui module). Try `exec hello`.

commands.name: fg
commands.summary: bring a job to the foreground.
commands.details:
exec hello   ... Ctrl+Z        hello is stopped, the prompt is back
  fg                             hello carries on; the shell waits
                                 Ctrl+C ends it, Ctrl+Z stops it again

The job (default: the newest, `+` in `jobs`) gets SIGCONT if it was
stopped. When it ends, its exit record (core/exitlog) says how.
commands.uses: process_get_table / process_get_by_pid / process_kill (core/process), scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), signal_send / signal_pending / signal_clear / signal_name (core/signal), exitlog_take (core/exitlog), sys_sleep / sys_sleep_interruptible (syscalls/sleep), atoi, ui.

commands.name: jobs
commands.summary: the programs this shell started that still exist.
commands.details:
[1]   Running   worker (PID 5)
  [2]-  Stopped   hello (PID 7)
  [3]+  Running   pause (PID 9)

A job is a child of the shell's process (spawn, exec &, nohup, a
stopped `exec`), numbered in the order they were started. `+` is the
newest (what fg/bg take by default), `-` the one before. There is no
job table: the process table already knows every child and its state.
commands.uses: process_get_table (core/process), scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), ui.

commands.name: kill
commands.summary: stop a process, or send it a signal.
commands.details:
kill 7               end PID 7 at once (SIGKILL)
  kill -TERM 7         send SIGTERM (also -15, -SIGTERM, -s TERM)
  kill -STOP 7         freeze it; `kill -CONT 7` lets it carry on
  kill -l              list every signal; `kill -l 15` names one

Without a signal UzOS's kill sends SIGKILL, not SIGTERM as Linux does:
a ring 0 program (spawn, exec) only looks at its signals when it
chooses, so SIGTERM might never stop it. A ring 3 program gets any
signal delivered on its next return to ring 3: its handler runs, or
the default action (most of them end it).

Why the command checks almost nothing itself: the real rules live in
kill_guard (inside process_kill) and signal_permission, so a syscall
or another module cannot skip them.
commands.uses: process_kill / process_get_by_pid (core/process), signal_send / signal_number / signal_name / signal_default_action (core/signal), def_signal_allowed (security/signal_abuse/defence/signal_permission), arg_next (lib/args), atoi (lib/stdlib), ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: killall
commands.summary: signal every process called
commands.details:
exactly 'name'.

  killall worker           end every "worker"
  killall -CONT worker     let every stopped "worker" carry on

Like `pkill -x name`. The default is SIGKILL, as for UzOS's `kill`;
the gates are the same (kill_guard / signal_permission), and the shell
itself is never hit.
commands.uses: process_get_table / process_kill / process_caller_uid (core/process), scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), signal_send / signal_number / signal_name (core/signal), def_signal_allowed (security/signal_abuse/defence/signal_permission), arg_next, ui.

commands.name: nohup
commands.summary: run it so that logout does not end it.
commands.details:
nohup sleep 300     [1] sleep (PID 6), ignoring SIGHUP
  logout              every other job ends with SIGHUP; this one lives

When a terminal session ends, its jobs get SIGHUP ("hang up"), whose
default action ends them (process_hangup, called by logout). nohup
starts the command in a background child that IGNORES SIGHUP. An
ignored signal stays ignored in everything that child starts, so the
whole command is safe.
commands.uses: nohup_start_child (start_child.c, this folder), SIGHUP / SIG_IGN (core/signal), ui.

commands.name: pgrep
commands.summary: find processes by name.
commands.details:
pgrep work          PIDs of every process whose name CONTAINS "work"
  pgrep -x worker     ...whose name IS "worker"
  pgrep -l -u guest . guest's processes, with their names

Linux's pgrep takes a regular expression; UzOS's matches a piece of
the name ("." matches anything, as the regex would). Zombies are left out.
commands.uses: process_get_table (core/process), users_find_name (user_management), strstr-like matching (in this file), arg_next, ui.

commands.name: pidof
commands.summary: the PIDs of the processes called exactly so.
commands.details:
pidof kernel_main idle     ->  2 1

All on one line, newest first, as Linux prints them. Zombies are left out.
commands.uses: process_get_table (core/process), arg_next, strcmp, ui.

commands.name: pkill
commands.summary: signal by name.
commands.details:
pkill work            end every process whose name contains "work"
  pkill -STOP -x worker freeze every "worker"
  pkill -u guest .      end all of guest's processes (root only)

The default is SIGKILL, as for UzOS's `kill` (a ring 0 program only
looks at other signals when it chooses). Each one goes through the
same gates as `kill`: kill_guard / signal_permission. The shell
itself is never hit.
commands.uses: process_get_table / process_kill / process_caller_uid (core/process), scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), signal_send / signal_number / signal_name (core/signal), def_signal_allowed (security/signal_abuse/defence/signal_permission), users_find_name (user_management), arg_next, ui.

commands.name: proccalls
commands.summary: call the process syscalls from
commands.details:
ring 3, check each answer.

The syscalls of process_management are meant for user programs, so
the honest test is a user program. Each GROUP is one ring 3 program
(a .s file in this folder), run as user 1 (guest) through usertask.
It goes through its syscalls with int 0x80 (the [syscall] trace shows
each one) and leaves every answer in the usertask mailbox. This
command prints them next to what a correct kernel answers:

  sigaction(USR1, h1)        0 ok    old handler            0 ok
  ...
  signals: 49 of 49 answers as expected

Some answers are refusals on purpose (-1): catching SIGKILL, a
handler inside the kernel, a forged rt_sigreturn.

  proccalls            every group
  proccalls signals    one group: signals, prctl, wait, session, timers
commands.uses: usertask_start / usertask_wait / usertask_mailbox (process_management/core/usertask), strcmp (lib/string), ui_* (ui).

commands.name: procinfo
commands.summary: everything the kernel knows about
commands.details:
one process, read straight from its process_t.

  PID 5  worker  S (sleeping)  user root
  family   parent 2  group 2  session 2  thread group 5
  time     started 12 s ago, CPU 0.01 s user + 0.03 s kernel
  sched    nice 0, priority 4, policy 0
  ---- details: its owner and root only (hidepid) ----
  cwd      /home/root
  files    3 open: 0 1 2
  signals  pending 00000000  blocked 00000000  ignored ...  caught ...
  timers   none
  altstack none
  prctl    pdeathsig 0  dumpable 1  no_new_privs 0  subreaper 0
  kernel   stack 00123000  esp 00123F80  entry 00104A2C (kptr_hide)

The first lines are for everyone (`ps` shows them too). The details
are asked of hidepid, and every kernel address goes through kptr_hide,
so a normal user sees zeros there.
commands.uses: process_get_by_pid / process_caller_uid / scheduler_get_current_process (core/process, core/scheduler), vfs_path_of (filesystem_management), users_name (user_management), timer_ticks / TIMER_HZ (device_management), def_hidepid_visible, def_kptr_show (security/), atoi, ui_*.

commands.name: pstree
commands.summary: the processes as a family tree.
commands.details:
pstree -p
  idle(1)
   |-kernel_main(2)
   |  |-worker(5)
   |  `-sleep(6)
   `-flood_target(9)       an orphan: its parent ended, PID 1 took it

The tree follows process_t.ppid. A process whose parent is gone is
re-parented when the parent ends (process_ended: to a subreaper, or
PID 1), so every branch hangs from a living process. Without -p the
PIDs are left out; with a pid, only that branch is drawn.
commands.uses: process_get_table / process_get_by_pid (core/process), atoi, ui.

commands.name: pwdx
commands.summary: where each process is working.
commands.details:
pwdx 2 5      2: /home/root
                5: /tmp

A process's directory says what its user is doing, so it is shown
only to its owner and root (hidepid).
commands.uses: process_get_by_pid / process_caller_uid (core/process), vfs_path_of (filesystem_management), def_hidepid_visible (security/proc_info_leak/defence/hidepid), arg_next, atoi, ui.

commands.name: setsid
commands.summary: run it in a session of its own.
commands.details:
setsid spawn        the worker's session is not the shell's
  logout              the shell's session hangs up; this one does not

A session is a login's group of process groups (process_t.sid). The
child becomes the leader of a NEW session and a new process group
(sid = pgid = its pid), like setsid() in Unix, so nothing that is sent
to the shell's session or group (SIGHUP at logout, kill(-pgid))
reaches it, nor anything it starts.
commands.uses: setsid_start_child (start_child.c, this folder), ui.

commands.name: sleep
commands.summary: pause the shell. Ctrl+C ends it early.
commands.uses: sys_sleep_interruptible (syscalls/sleep), atoi (lib/stdlib), ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: spawn
commands.summary: start a background worker process.
commands.details:
The worker prints a heartbeat 3 times, 3 seconds apart, then exits.
Meanwhile the shell keeps working: that is multitasking.
commands.uses: process_create (core/process), sys_sleep and sys_exit (syscalls/), sys_getpid to print its own PID, ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: testuser
commands.summary: run a tiny program in ring 3.
commands.details:
testuser         calls write, getpid, uptime, mmap, munmap, exit via int 0x80
  testuser null    writes to address 0: the page fault kills only it
  testuser badptr  passes write() an unmapped buffer: only that call fails

The program is copied to the user pages and dropped to ring 3 by
usertask (core/usertask). From there it can only reach the kernel
through int 0x80; each call is traced on the screen by the syscall
handler.
commands.uses: usertask_start (core/usertask), sys_sleep, ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: timeout
commands.summary: a time limit.
commands.details:
timeout 2 sleep 10       sleep ends after 2 s: "timed out"
  timeout -s INT 2 top     top gets SIGINT after 2 s (it stops itself)

The command runs in a child (start_child.c); the shell waits. When the
time is up the child gets the signal (default SIGTERM); if it still
runs one second later it is killed (SIGKILL), since a ring 0 command
only looks at the signals it wants. Ctrl+C ends it at once.
commands.uses: timeout_start_child (start_child.c, this folder), process_get_by_pid / process_kill (core/process), scheduler_get_current_process, signal_send / signal_number / signal_pending / signal_name (core/signal), sys_sleep_interruptible, timer_ticks / TIMER_HZ (device_management), arg_next, atoi, ui.

commands.name: wait
commands.summary: wait until jobs end.
commands.details:
spawn ; spawn ; wait       both workers end (9 s), then:
  [1] worker: exit code 0
  [2] worker: exit code 0

Without arguments: every job of the shell. Ctrl+C stops waiting (the
jobs keep running). How each one ended comes from its exit record
(core/exitlog), the same that wait4() reads.
commands.uses: process_get_table / process_get_by_pid (core/process), scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), exitlog_take (core/exitlog), signal_pending / signal_name (core/signal), sys_sleep / sys_sleep_interruptible (syscalls/sleep), arg_next, atoi, ui.

syscalls.name: exit
syscalls.summary: exit(code): end the calling process.
syscalls.details:
The exit code (low 8 bits) is kept as exit_status = code << 8, the
way wait() reports it (WEXITSTATUS).
syscalls.uses: process_exit_with() (core/process). The process becomes a zombie and never runs again; the reaper frees its slot and stack later.

syscalls.name: sleep
syscalls.summary: stop running for 'ms' milliseconds.
syscalls.details:
The process is marked SLEEPING with a tick count. The scheduler skips
it, and every timer tick counts it down; at 0 it becomes READY again.
Sleeping costs no CPU time, unlike a busy loop.

sys_sleep_interruptible() is the same, except that signal_send()
(core/signal) may wake the process early: Ctrl+C ends `sleep 30`.
syscalls.uses: the scheduler (current process, yield), def_sleep_ms_ticks (security/sleep_overflow/defence/sleep_bounds), cpu_irq_save (arch/x86/cpu), SIGINT bits (core/signal).

syscalls.name: getppid
syscalls.summary: return the caller's parent process id.

syscalls.name: setpgid
syscalls.summary: setpgid(pid, pgid): put a process in a process group.
syscalls.details:
pid 0 means the caller; pgid 0 means "a new group named by the pid".
session_check applies the POSIX rules: yourself or your child, within
your session, never a session leader, and only into a new group or
one that exists in that session.

syscalls.name: getpgid
syscalls.summary: getpgid(pid): return a process's group id.

syscalls.name: getpgrp
syscalls.summary: the caller's process-group id.

syscalls.name: setsid
syscalls.summary: the caller starts a new session and a new
syscalls.details:
process group, and becomes the leader of both (sid = pgid = its pid).
Returns the new session id, or -1 if the caller already leads a
process group (session_check: its group would be split in two).

syscalls.name: getsid
syscalls.summary: getsid(pid): return a process's session id.

syscalls.name: kill
syscalls.summary: kill(pid, sig): send a signal to one process or a group.
syscalls.details:
pid > 0    that process
  pid == 0   every process in my process group
  pid == -1  every process I may signal (not system ones, not myself)
  pid < -1   every process in group -pid

Each target is checked by signal_permission (your own process, or
CAP_KILL, never a system process). SIGKILL ends a process at once
(process_kill); sig 0 sends nothing, it only asks "may I?". Returns 0
if at least one process got it, -1 otherwise.
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process, process_get_by_pid / process_get_table / process_kill (core/process); signal_send, SIGKILL (core/signal); caps_has (security_management); def_signal_allowed (security/signal_abuse/defence/signal_permission).

syscalls.name: tkill
syscalls.summary: tkill(tid, sig): signal a single thread by its id.
syscalls.details:
In UzOS a thread IS a process (threads share a tgid, see clone), so a
tid is a pid. Same permission rule as kill. tkill is the old, less
safe interface; tgkill adds a thread-group check.
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process, process_get_by_pid, process_kill (core/process); signal_send, SIGKILL (core/signal); def_signal_allowed (signal_permission).

syscalls.name: tgkill
syscalls.summary: tgkill(tgid, tid, sig): signal a thread, but only if it
syscalls.details:
really belongs to thread group 'tgid'. This closes a tkill race: a tid
could be reused by another group between look-up and signal. Checking
the tgid makes sure you signal the thread you meant.
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process, process_get_by_pid, process_kill (core/process); signal_send, SIGKILL (core/signal); def_signal_allowed (signal_permission); process_t.tgid.

syscalls.name: pidfd_send_signal
syscalls.summary: pidfd_send_signal(pidfd, sig): send a signal
syscalls.details:
to the process a pidfd (pidfd_open) names.

This is Linux's fix for the kill() race: between finding a pid and
killing it, the process may end and the number may come back as
someone else. The pidfd names the process itself, so once it ended
this fails (-1, ESRCH) instead of hitting the next one. Same
permission rule as kill (signal_permission).
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), process_kill (core/process), pidfd_target (core/pidfd: pcb_generation inside), signal_send, SIGKILL (core/signal), def_signal_allowed (security/signal_abuse/defence/signal_permission).

syscalls.name: wait
syscalls.summary: block until one of the caller's children ends.
syscalls.details:
Returns the pid of a finished child, or -1 if the caller has none.
The child's record is taken from core/exitlog (the reaper wrote it),
so the same child is never reported twice; wait4() also gives the
exit status. Threads are not waited for.

syscalls.name: waitpid
syscalls.summary: waitpid(pid): block until a specific child ends.
syscalls.details:
Returns 'pid' once that child has ended (its record is taken from
core/exitlog), or -1 if it is not the caller's child (child_only).
wait4() is the same with the exit status and resource usage.
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process, process_get_by_pid (core/process), exitlog_take / exitlog_find (core/exitlog), sys_sleep (syscalls/sleep), def_wait_allowed (security/wait_steal/defence/child_only).

syscalls.name: waitid
syscalls.summary: waitid(idtype, id, infop, options): the richer wait.
syscalls.details:
P_ALL     any child            P_PID    the child 'id'
  P_PGID    any child in group 'id'      P_PIDFD  the child pidfd 'id' names

Fills 'infop' instead of a status word: who ended (pid, uid) and how
(code CLD_EXITED + exit code, or CLD_KILLED / CLD_DUMPED + the
signal). Returns the child's pid (Linux returns 0; UzOS gives the pid,
which infop->pid also holds), 0 with WNOHANG if none ended yet, -1 on
error. The record is taken from core/exitlog, like every wait.
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process, process_get_table / process_get_by_pid (core/process), exitlog_take / exitlog_find (core/exitlog), pidfd_target (core/pidfd), sys_sleep (syscalls/sleep), def_wait_allowed (security/wait_steal/defence/child_only), SIGCHLD.

syscalls.name: fork
syscalls.summary: needs per-process address spaces (see .h).
syscalls.uses: nothing (returns -1 until UzOS has separate address spaces).

syscalls.name: vfork
syscalls.summary: needs per-process address spaces (see .h).

syscalls.name: execve
syscalls.summary: in-place image replacement is not
syscalls.details: supported; the `exec` command loads ELF programs instead (see .h).

syscalls.name: execveat
syscalls.summary: same as execve (see .h).

syscalls.name: rt_sigaction
syscalls.summary: rt_sigaction(sig, act, oldact, sigsetsize).
syscalls.details:
Read and/or change what signal 'sig' does for the caller:
  act->handler   SIG_DFL (the default), SIG_IGN, or a function
  act->flags     SA_SIGINFO (3 arguments), SA_ONSTACK, SA_RESTORER,
                 SA_NODEFER, SA_RESETHAND
  act->mask      signals also blocked while the handler runs
Setting SIG_IGN (or a default of "ignore") throws away a pending one,
as Linux does. Returns 0, or -1 (bad signal, refused).

syscalls.name: rt_sigprocmask
syscalls.summary: rt_sigprocmask(how, set, oldset, sigsetsize).
syscalls.details:
A blocked signal stays pending until it is unblocked; then it is
delivered on the next return to ring 3. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can never
be blocked (they are taken out of 'set' silently, as in Linux).
A sigset is 4 or 8 bytes (Linux uses 8); UzOS uses the low 32 bits.

syscalls.name: rt_sigpending
syscalls.summary: rt_sigpending(set, sigsetsize): the signals sent
syscalls.details: to the caller and not delivered yet (in practice: the blocked ones).

syscalls.name: rt_sigsuspend
syscalls.summary: rt_sigsuspend(mask, sigsetsize).
syscalls.details:
"Unblock these and wait" in ONE step: the blocked mask becomes 'mask'
until a signal arrives, so a signal can never slip in between an
unblock and a pause(). The old mask comes back after the handler
(delivery saves it in the frame; rt_sigreturn restores it). Always
returns -1 (EINTR), like Linux. For ring 3 programs.

syscalls.name: rt_sigtimedwait
syscalls.summary: rt_sigtimedwait(set, info, timeout, sigsetsize).
syscalls.details:
Wait until one of the signals in 'set' is pending, then TAKE it: no
handler runs, the signal number is returned and 'info' says who sent
it. The signals in 'set' are normally blocked first, so they wait for
this call instead of being delivered. timeout 0 = wait for ever.

  returns  the signal number
           -1 when the time is up (EAGAIN), or another signal that is
           not blocked arrived (EINTR: it is delivered on the way out)
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), sigqueue_take, signal_deliverable (core/signal), sys_sleep (syscalls/sleep), timer_ticks (device_management), cpu_irq_save, def_sleep_time_ticks (security/sleep_overflow/defence/sleep_bounds).

syscalls.name: rt_sigqueueinfo
syscalls.summary: rt_sigqueueinfo(pid, sig, info): sigqueue(3).
syscalls.details:
Like kill(), but the signal carries info->value, and every one
arrives: two queued SIGUSR1s run the handler twice, with each value.
Only the value is taken from 'info': the kernel writes who sent it
(pid, uid) and why (SI_QUEUE) itself, so a sender cannot pretend to
be the kernel or another process.

Same permission rule as kill() (signal_permission); the queue has a
share per user (sigqueue_limit, inside sigqueue_add).
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process, process_get_by_pid (core/process), sigqueue_add / sigqueue_take / signal_send_info (core/signal), def_signal_allowed (security/signal_abuse/defence/signal_permission).

syscalls.name: rt_tgsigqueueinfo
syscalls.summary: rt_tgsigqueueinfo(tgid, tid, sig, info).
syscalls.details:
rt_sigqueueinfo() for one THREAD: 'tid' must belong to thread group
'tgid' (the same safety check tgkill() makes, so a reused tid can
never hit the wrong program). Value, sender and permission as in
rt_sigqueueinfo().
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process, process_get_by_pid (core/process), sigqueue_add / sigqueue_take / signal_send_info (core/signal), def_signal_allowed (security/signal_abuse/defence/signal_permission).

syscalls.name: rt_sigreturn
syscalls.summary: end a signal handler.
syscalls.details:
The handler's 'ret' took it to the frame's trampoline (or its
restorer), which runs `mov eax, 76 ; int 0x80`. ESP now points just
past frame->ret, so the frame is at ESP - 4. Every register saved in
it is put back into 'regs', so the iret lands exactly where the
program was when the signal came, with its old blocked mask.

The frame is in the program's own memory: it may have been edited or
forged. sigframe_check decides what may come back; a refused frame
ends the program with SIGSEGV.

Returns the restored EAX (the syscall handler writes it to regs->eax).
syscalls.uses: scheduler_get_current_process (core/scheduler), process_exit_with (core/process), sigframe_t (core/signal), def_user_range_ok (memory_management defence user_ptr_bounds), def_sigframe_check (security/sigreturn_forgery/defence/sigframe_check), ui (a line saying why the program was ended).

syscalls.name: sigaltstack
syscalls.summary: sigaltstack(ss, old_ss).
syscalls.details:
A handler set with SA_ONSTACK runs on this stack instead of the
program's own. That is how a program handles SIGSEGV from a stack
overflow: its own stack is full, the alternate one is not.

  ss->flags = SS_DISABLE    no alternate stack any more
  otherwise                 [ss->sp, ss->sp + ss->size) becomes it:
                            at least MINSIGSTKSZ, mapped user memory
old_ss gets the previous one, flags SS_ONSTACK if a handler is
running on it now. While running on it, it cannot be changed.
'user_esp' is the caller's stack pointer (to tell if it is on it).

syscalls.name: pause
syscalls.summary: sleep until a signal that is not blocked comes.
syscalls.details:
Ignored signals never wake it (they are thrown away when sent). It
always returns -1 (EINTR); the signal is delivered on the way out, so
its handler has run when the program sees -1. A deadly signal ends
the program instead.

syscalls.name: alarm
syscalls.summary: alarm(seconds): send SIGALRM to the caller later.
syscalls.details:
A new alarm replaces the old one; 0 cancels it. Returns the seconds
that were left of the old alarm (rounded up), 0 if there was none.
alarm() is ITIMER_REAL (setitimer) without an interval: the countdown
is process_t.itimer_value[ITIMER_REAL]; signal_tick() (core/signal)
counts it down on every timer tick and sends SIGALRM at 0.

syscalls.name: prctl
syscalls.summary: prctl(option, arg2): read or change one setting of the
syscalls.details:
calling process.

  PR_SET_NAME / PR_GET_NAME    the name `ps` shows (name_guard checks it)
  PR_SET_PDEATHSIG / GET       a signal for us when our parent ends
  PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER / GET orphans below us are re-parented to us
  PR_SET_DUMPABLE / GET        may others inspect us (procinfo, ptrace)
  PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS / GET    exec can never raise our rights; cannot
                               be turned off again

syscalls.name: wait4

Which child (as in Linux):
  pid > 0     that child          pid == -1   any child
  pid == 0    any child in my process group
  pid < -1    any child in process group -pid

When one has ended, its record is TAKEN from core/exitlog (the reaper
wrote it), so each child is reported once:
  *wstatus = how it ended:  exit(n) -> n << 8,  signal s -> s (| 0x80 core)
  *rusage  = the CPU time and context switches it (and its children) used
  returns its pid
-1 = no such child (ECHILD), not your child (child_only), or a signal
came while waiting (EINTR). With WNOHANG, 0 = children run, none ended.
Threads (clone CLONE_THREAD) are not waited for, as in Linux.

one 4 KiB kernel stack), and the context switches. Returns 0 or -1.

syscalls.name: times
syscalls.summary: times(buf): where the caller's CPU time went, in ticks.
syscalls.details:
UzOS's timer ticks 100 times a second, the same as Linux's clock tick
(USER_HZ), so the numbers need no conversion. Returns the ticks since
boot: a program measures elapsed time by calling times() twice.

syscalls.name: pidfd_open
syscalls.summary: pidfd_open(pid, flags): get a handle on a process.
syscalls.details:
The handle (a file descriptor) names exactly this process for ever:
pidfd_send_signal, pidfd_getfd and waitid(P_PIDFD) use it, and they
fail once the process has ended, instead of reaching whoever comes
next. close() it like any file. Returns the descriptor, or -1.

syscalls.summary: pidfd_getfd(pidfd, targetfd, flags).
syscalls.details:
The process named by 'pidfd' has file 'targetfd' open; give the
caller a descriptor for the same file (same node, same flags, the
offset it had). That is like reading the other process's memory, so it
needs ptrace rights (pidfd_handle). Returns the new descriptor or -1.

syscalls.name: nanosleep
syscalls.summary: nanosleep(req, rem): sleep this long.
syscalls.details:
The time is rounded UP to whole timer ticks (10 ms): asking for 1 ns
sleeps one tick, never less than asked. A signal that is not blocked
ends the sleep early: then it returns -1 (EINTR) and *rem says how
much was left, so the program can sleep again for the rest.
Returns 0, or -1 for a bad time (sleep_bounds) or a signal.

syscalls.name: clock_nanosleep
syscalls.summary: clock_nanosleep(clock, flags, req, rem).
syscalls.details:

  clock   CLOCK_MONOTONIC (since boot) or CLOCK_REALTIME (the date)
  flags   0: sleep for 'req'     TIMER_ABSTIME: sleep UNTIL 'req'

          program took between two sleeps)
A moment in the past returns at once. Like Linux, it returns the error
number itself: 0, CNS_EINVAL (bad clock / time), CNS_EINTR (a signal;
*rem = what was left, for a relative sleep).

syscalls.summary: setitimer(which, new, old): arm or disarm a timer.
syscalls.details:
which   ITIMER_REAL     wall clock      -> SIGALRM
          ITIMER_VIRTUAL  my ring 3 CPU   -> SIGVTALRM
          ITIMER_PROF     all my CPU      -> SIGPROF
  new     value = when it first fires (0 disarms), interval = then

  old     what it was set to before (time left, interval)

syscalls.name: getitimer
syscalls.summary: getitimer(which, cur): read an interval timer.
syscalls.details:
cur->value is the time left until it fires (0 = not armed), in whole
ticks of 10 ms; cur->interval is how often it fires again. Returns 0,
or -1 for a bad 'which'.

security.story: Break out of a container - a process boxed in by namespaces, cgroups and dropped capabilities - to reach the host, via a leaked capability, a shared mount, or a kernel bug.

security.what: create processes in a loop until every slot is used
security.story: A fork bomb creates processes in a loop. In a real one every child loops too, so the number doubles until the process table is full. Then nothing else can start, not even a shell to stop it.

2. the last RESERVED_FOR_ROOT free slots are for root only

security.what: rt_sigaction: catch SIGKILL, ignore SIGSTOP, handler in the kernel
security.story: `rt_sigaction()` says "when signal N comes, run the code at address X". A program that catches SIGKILL or ignores SIGSTOP can never be stopped. A handler address inside the kernel asks the kernel to jump into its own code whenever the program sends itself a signal.

1. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored
2. a handler is SIG_DFL, SIG_IGN, or a user-space address
3. with SA_RESTORER, the restorer is a user-space address

security.what: read kernel stack / ESP / entry addresses of a process
security.story: An exploit needs to know where things are. `procinfo` knows a process's kernel stack, its saved stack pointer and the kernel function it runs: handed to a normal user, that is a map for an attack.

security.what: enter ring 3 with a stack pointer into kernel memory
security.story: `switch_to_user_mode(eip, esp)` drops the CPU to ring 3 with the stack pointer it is given. User code then pushes and writes to that stack freely. If `esp` points into a **kernel** stack, user code can overwrite the kernel's saved registers and return addresses, and so make the kernel run its code.

security.what: call process_kill() directly to destroy a system process
security.story: UzOS has two system processes: `idle` (PID 1) and `kernel_main` (PID 2, the shell). An early version protected PID 1 only inside the `kill` shell command. But `process_kill()` is a normal kernel function: a syscall or any module can call it directly, and the shell check never runs.

defence.called: process_kill() (core/process), before anything is changed.

1. the target must exist
2. system processes (idle, kernel_main) can never be killed
3. CAP_KILL (root) may kill any other process; a user only its own
defence.why: the guard sits inside process_kill(), not in the `kill` command, so every caller passes through it.

security.what: a crafted ELF file loads over the kernel or overflows the loader
security.story: `exec <file>` loads an ELF program. The loader copies bytes to the addresses the **file** names and jumps to the entry point the **file** names. Whoever writes the file controls those numbers.

builds each crafted header in memory and runs it through the same checks elf_load_and_run() uses; then checks that a normal program still passes

defence.fix: check every ELF header field before the loader uses it
defence.called: elf_load_and_run() (core/elf), after reading the header and again after reading the program headers.
defence.rules:
header   - ELF magic, 32-bit, little-endian, executable, i386,
1..ELF_MAX_PHDRS program headers of the right size,
entry point in user space
segments - file size <= memory size, and the whole range
[vaddr, vaddr + memsz) inside user space, no wrap
defence.why: every number in an ELF file comes from whoever wrote the file. Without checks, a segment could load over the kernel at 1 MiB, wrap around the end of memory, or overflow the loader's array.

security.what: leave children orphaned and hope nobody reaps them
security.story: Let a parent exit before its children. Those orphans, on a system that reaps a zombie only when its parent calls `wait()`, could sit dead forever and leak process slots.

defence.fix: a global reaper frees every zombie, so an orphan never leaks a slot
defence.called: the reaper (core/scheduler, defence reaper), which runs over the whole table and collects any ZOMBIE, parent alive or not.
defence.why: on Linux an orphan is re-parented to init (pid 1) so it is reaped. UzOS has a global reaper instead, which reaches every zombie directly; the result is the same - no orphan leaks a process slot. (zombie_leak/reaper is the same reaper seen from the "parent never reaped me" angle.)
defence.story: Linux re-parents orphans to init (pid 1); UzOS uses a **global reaper** that collects every zombie by its state, parent alive or not - same result, no leak. (See also zombie_leak, the same reaper from the "parent never reaped me" angle.)

security.what: setpgid into another session's group, or pull a stranger into yours
security.story: A process group gets its terminal's signals (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z, SIGHUP at logout), and `kill(-pgid)` signals the whole group. If `setpgid()` let anyone into any group, a process could join another login's group, or pull a stranger's process into its own and then `kill(-group)` it.

defence.fix: setpgid/setsid: groups stay in their session (POSIX rules)
defence.called: sys_setpgid() and sys_setsid() (syscalls/), before a process changes group or session.
defence.why: a process group is what gets a terminal's signals (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z, SIGHUP at logout) and what kill(-pgid) hits. Joining another session's group lets a process receive or dodge those signals as part of someone else's login; pulling a stranger into your group lets you kill(-pgid) it.

security.what: a stale pid / handle signals whoever took the process's place
security.story: `pgrep worker` → `1234` ... the worker ends ... `kill 1234`. Where PIDs wrap around (Linux, `pid_max`), 1234 may now be a different process, and it gets the signal. UzOS never reuses a PID (`pid_bounds`), but it does reuse process **slots**: a handle that only remembered the slot would have the same race.

defence.fix: pidfds name one live process; getfd needs ptrace rights
defence.called: sys_pidfd_open (open), sys_pidfd_getfd (getfd). Every use of a handle also goes through pidfd_target() (core/pidfd), which asks pcb_generation whether the handle's process still lives.
defence.rules:
1. a handle is made only for a live process (no zombie, no
system process)
2. a handle never moves: once its process ends, every use
fails (ESRCH) instead of reaching the next process
3. pidfd_getfd copies another process's open file: it needs
ptrace rights (your own dumpable process, or CAP_PTRACE)
defence.why: `pgrep worker` then `kill 1234` is a race: between the two the process may end and, where PIDs wrap (Linux, pid_max), 1234 may now be someone else. A handle closes the gap. Copying a file descriptor is like reading the other process's memory, so it is guarded the same way (Linux: PTRACE_MODE_ATTACH).

security.what: the PID counter wraps around and reuses a live PID
security.story: `next_pid` counts up: 1, 2, 3, ... A 32-bit counter wraps after `0xFFFFFFFF` back to 0, then 1, and PID 1 (`idle`) is still alive. Two processes would then share a PID, and `kill 1` or `process_get_by_pid(1)` would hit whichever one comes first in the table.

4 billion creations is too many, so it asks the guard about the edge PIDs: 1, 0xFFFFFEFF, 0xFFFFFF00, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0

defence.fix: stop handing out PIDs before the counter can wrap
defence.called: process_create() for the next PID, process_kill() for the target.
defence.why: PIDs come from a counter that only goes up. If it wrapped past 0xFFFFFFFF back to 1, a new process could get the PID of a live one, and `kill 7` might hit the wrong process. Running out of PIDs is a visible error; a reused PID is a silent one.

security.what: a user reads root's process details: directory, files, signals
security.story: The kernel knows each process's working directory, open files and signal masks. A tool that shows them to anyone (`procinfo`, `pwdx`, `/proc/<pid>/status`) tells a stranger which files you are editing.

modes.text: starts root's secret_job and user 1's my_job, asks hidepid as user 1 about both
kills both

defence.fix: process details (cwd, files, signals) only for the owner and root
defence.called: procinfo and pwdx (commands/), /proc/<pid>/status (filesystem_management core/procfs), before they show the details of a process.
defence.why: a process's working directory, open files and signal masks tell a stranger what its user is doing: which files they edit, where their secrets are. Linux has the same rule as the /proc mount option hidepid=invisible (and ptrace_may_access).

security.what: deny service by exhausting process slots or CPU (umbrella)
security.story: Deny service through process abuse: spawn endlessly, fill the process table, or hog the CPU so real work never runs.

defence.fix: per-user process and CPU caps keep one account from starving the rest
defence.called: the limits that already do the work - slot_quota in process_create (process count) and the CPU quotas / RLIMIT_CPU in cpu_management (CPU time).
defence.why: "process-based DoS" is the umbrella over fork bombs, process- table exhaustion and CPU hogs. Each already has its own live defence; this pair names the umbrella and points at them.
defence.story: The answer is limits, which already exist as live defences: per-user process caps (`fork_bomb`/`slot_quota`) and CPU quotas (`cpu_exhaustion`/`starvation` in cpu_management). This pair names the umbrella and points at the real enforcement.

security.what: redirect a running program to attacker-chosen code (concept)
security.story: Redirect a running program to attacker-chosen code by corrupting a return address or function pointer.

defence.fix: concept: the kernel sets entry/return; full CFI is compiler+hardware
defence.called: the kernel sets each process's entry point and its ring-3 return frame (core/usertask); ring 3 cannot rewrite them.
defence.why: hijacking redirects a program to run attacker-chosen code (overwrite a return address or a function pointer). Full CFI checks every indirect jump/return against a legal target - a compiler and hardware feature. UzOS's part is isolation: no one can reach into the kernel's saved frames to redirect them.
defence.story: True CFI - checking every indirect call/return against a legal target - is a compiler and hardware feature. UzOS's part is isolation: the kernel owns each process's entry and ring-3 return frames, out of ring 3's reach.

security.what: write code into another process's memory and run it (concept)
security.story: Write code or data into a running process's memory (ptrace `POKETEXT`, `/proc/<pid>/mem`) and make it execute.

defence.fix: concept: ring3 is walled off; full per-process isolation needs own AS
defence.called: the CPU, via the PAGE_USER bit, for ring 3 code (core/umem).
defence.why: injection writes code or data into another process's memory. The real barrier is a separate address space per process. UzOS isolates ring 3 from the kernel, but its kernel-mode tasks share one address space, so full isolation here is a concept - the lesson is what a complete barrier requires.
defence.story: The real barrier is a separate address space per process. UzOS walls ring 3 off from the kernel (the `PAGE_USER` bit) but its kernel-mode tasks share one address space, so a full demo is a concept here - the lesson is what complete isolation requires.

security.story: People and tools find processes by name. Malware renames itself to look like part of the OS (`kernel_main`), so nobody dares to kill it. A name with an escape sequence repaints the screen of the admin who runs `ps`.

1. printable characters only (0x20..0x7E): no ANSI escapes,
no newlines that would fake extra lines in `ps`
2. not empty
3. a normal process may not take a system process's name
("idle", "kernel_main")

security.what: attach a debugger to a process you do not own to read its memory
security.story: Use a debugging interface (`ptrace`) to attach to a process you don't own and read its registers and memory - keys, passwords, tokens.

defence.why: a debugger sees and can change every byte of the traced process. Without an owner check, ptrace is a read/write window into anyone's secrets - the classic way one account steals another's keys. Linux restricts it (Yama ptrace_scope).
defence.story: UzOS has no `ptrace()` yet; this is the gate one would need: a system process is off limits, a debug-capable user may attach to any other, and otherwise you may only debug a process you own (as Linux does with Yama's `ptrace_scope`).

security.what: send a signal to another user's or the kernel's processes
security.story: Send a signal (SIGINT, SIGKILL, ...) to a process you don't own, or to one of the kernel's processes, to stop or disturb it.

defence.fix: a signal reaches only your own processes (CAP_KILL for others)
defence.called: the signal-sending paths (the `kill` command today; the kill / tkill / tgkill syscalls when they are added), before a signal reaches another process.
defence.why: a signal can stop or disturb a process. Without an owner check any user could SIGINT or kill another user's work, or poke at the kernel's own processes. (kill_guard is the same idea for the `kill` command; this is the general rule for every signal.)
defence.story: The signal-sending paths ask `def_signal_allowed` first: a system process is never signalled, a CAP_KILL holder may signal any other, and otherwise you may signal only your own processes. (`kill_guard` is the same idea for the `kill` command; this is the general rule for every signal path.)

security.what: queue signals to a target that never takes them, until the pool is full
security.story: `rt_sigqueueinfo()` sends a signal with a value. The kernel must keep every queued value until it is delivered. A target that blocks the signal never takes them, so a user who keeps queueing fills the pool, and no one else can queue a signal any more.

defence.why: a queued signal carries a value, so each one needs kernel memory until it is delivered. The pool has 64 entries for everyone. A target that blocks the signal never takes them, so without a cap one user fills the pool and nobody else can queue a signal any more. Linux has the same limit (RLIMIT_SIGPENDING, `ulimit -i`).

security.what: SROP: rt_sigreturn with a forged or edited frame, to get IOPL 3
security.story: A signal handler returns through `rt_sigreturn`, which loads **every** register from the frame on the program's own stack. If the kernel trusts that memory, a program can write any values it likes and call `rt_sigreturn`: "Sigreturn Oriented Programming". With IOPL = 3 in EFLAGS, ring 3 may run `cli` and `in`/`out`, so it owns the hardware.

defence.fix: rt_sigreturn restores only a frame the kernel pushed; never IOPL
defence.called: sys_rt_sigreturn() (syscalls/rt_sigreturn), before it loads the saved registers into the CPU.
defence.rules:
1. there is a handler frame the kernel pushed, and 'frame' is
the newest one (each frame comes back once)
2. the saved EIP and ESP are user-space addresses
3. EFLAGS keeps only the bits a program may set itself:
IOPL, NT and VM are cleared, IF is set
defence.why: rt_sigreturn loads EVERY register from memory the program owns. That is "Sigreturn Oriented Programming" (SROP): forge a frame, call rt_sigreturn without any signal, and the kernel sets whatever registers you wrote. EFLAGS with IOPL 3 lets a ring 3 program run cli and in/out: it owns the hardware. Rule 1 refuses a frame no signal made; rule 3 still strips IOPL from a real frame the handler changed.

security.what: huge or malformed times wrap the kernel's tick arithmetic
security.story: Times from a program become timer ticks. In 32-bit arithmetic big ones wrap: `nanosleep(42949673 s)` becomes 0.3 s, `sleep(0xFFFFFFFF ms)` becomes 0. A protective timeout fires at once; a "far future" deadline is already past. Malformed times (`nsec >= 1e9`, negative) are nonsense.

defence.fix: times become ticks in 64 bits, rounded up, capped; bad ones refused
defence.called: sys_sleep / sys_sleep_interruptible (ms), nanosleep, clock_nanosleep, setitimer, rt_sigtimedwait (timespec / timeval) - every place a program's time becomes ticks.
defence.rules:
1. a negative time, or nsec >= 1e9 (usec >= 1e6), is refused
(Linux: EINVAL)
2. the conversion is done in 64 bits and rounded UP: 1 ns
still waits a tick, never 0
3. the result is capped at SLEEP_MAX_TICKS (2^31 - 1, ~248
days): "deadline - now" always fits a signed 32-bit number
defence.why: sec * 100 in 32 bits wraps: 42949673 s becomes 0.3 s, and "(ms + 9) / 10" with ms = 0xFFFFFFFF becomes 0. A program that asked to sleep for months returns at once, a timeout that should protect something expires immediately, and a wrapped deadline can look already passed - or never come.

security.what: recursion runs off the bottom of a 4 KiB stack into the heap
security.story: Every process gets a 4 KiB stack from the kernel heap. Each function call pushes a frame. Deep recursion keeps pushing below the stack's bottom, and the x86 CPU does not stop it: the next heap object is silently overwritten. Nothing crashes right away, which makes this worse than a crash.

measures one frame with an 8-deep recursion, then asks the guard about an ESP one push below a stack's bottom

defence.fix: retire a process whose stack pointer left its own stack
defence.called: scheduler_yield() (core/scheduler), on every task switch, with the real ESP of the running process.
defence.why: the CPU does not stop a push below the bottom of a 4 KiB stack; it silently overwrites the heap. This check notices it at the next switch and retires the process. A stronger fix is a "guard page": an unmapped page below each stack, so the very first bad push faults. That needs per-process paging first.

security.what: arm every interval timer of many processes at 100 Hz
security.story: Each process has three interval timers. Armed at the shortest interval, each makes the kernel count, signal and deliver 100 times a second. A user who arms all of them in every process they may have turns the timer interrupt into their private worker.
security.tryIt:
seclab attack timer_flood live
procinfo <pid of a ticker>     # timers: real 10 ms (every 10 ms), ...
seclab repair

defence.fix: a user may have at most 8 periodic interval timers armed
defence.called: sys_setitimer() (syscalls/setitimer), before it arms a timer with an interval.
defence.why: every firing is work for the KERNEL: count down, send a signal, wake a process, deliver it. A user who arms timers in all their processes at the fastest rate makes the timer tick spend its time on them: everyone else's programs slow down. Linux bounds the same thing with RLIMIT_SIGPENDING and the POSIX timer limits.

security.what: swap a resource between the check and the use of it
security.story: TOCTOU = Time Of Check to Time Of Use. Check "is this file mine?", and in the gap before you open it an attacker swaps it for a symlink to a secret - which you then open with your own rights.

defence.fix: check and use in one uninterruptible step; no check-then-use gap
defence.called: the rule every check-then-use site should follow (e.g. open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL instead of "does it exist?" then create).
defence.why: TOCTOU = Time Of Check to Time Of Use. If you test a file's owner and THEN open it, an attacker can swap the file in the gap and you open theirs. One atomic step removes the gap.
defence.story: Never split the check from the use: do both in one step the kernel can't be interrupted in (open with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`, then act on the file descriptor, not the name). No gap, no race.

security.what: a reused process slot hands its old owner's data to the new process
security.story: The process table has 64 slots that are reused again and again. `process_create()` writes the fields it needs (pid, name, uid, stack). Any field it does **not** write (`cwd`, `fd_table`, `fd_offset`, ...) keeps the previous owner's value. The new process then "has" files it never opened, and a stale `cwd` pointer can crash the filesystem code.

modes.text: counts free slots that still hold old data
writes fake old data (cwd, fd 3) into the next free slot, creates a process there, counts what survived
kills the probe process

security.tryIt:

seclab repair

defence.fix: zero a process slot before giving it to a new process
defence.called: process_init() for every slot, process_create() for the new one.
defence.why: slots are reused many times. A field the new owner does not set (cwd, open files, ...) would still hold the old owner's value: an information leak, and a stale pointer waiting to crash. "Every field is either mine or zero" is easy to trust.

security.what: keep a process pointer across its death; reach the slot's newcomer
security.story: The process table has 64 slots, and they are reused. Kernel code that keeps a `process_t *` while it sleeps (a wait, a pidfd, a debugger) can wake up after that process ended and its slot went to a new one. The old pointer then signals, inspects or reaps the **newcomer**.
security.tryIt:
seclab attack use_after_exit live
audit
seclab repair

defence.fix: a saved process reference is checked: same slot, same pid, same life
defence.called: core/pidfd, on every use of a pidfd (pidfd_send_signal, pidfd_getfd, waitid P_PIDFD); anyone who keeps a process across a sleep.
defence.why: the process table has 64 slots and they are reused. A kernel path that keeps a process_t * while it sleeps may wake up to find the process gone and its slot given to someone else; a signal, an exit status or a permission check would then hit the newcomer. Linux keeps a reference count on the task (and struct pid) for the same reason.

security.what: wait4() for another process's child and take its exit status
security.story: An exit status says what a program did, and it is collected **once**. A stranger who could `wait4()` for your child would read it first, and you would never see it.
security.tryIt:
seclab attack wait_steal live
audit

defence.fix: only a process's parent may wait for it and take its exit status
defence.called: sys_wait4, sys_waitpid, sys_waitid, when the caller names a pid; exitlog_take() (core/exitlog) also hands a record only to the parent it names.
defence.why: an exit status tells what a program did (which test failed, whether a login was right) and collecting it is a one-time event: whoever takes it, the real parent never sees it. A stranger who could wait for your child would steal both.

security.what: finished processes never give back their slot or stack
security.story: When a process function returns, the process is finished, but it cannot free its own stack while still standing on it. It becomes a **zombie**: it never runs again, yet still holds its slot and 4 KiB stack. An early version of UzOS never freed zombies, so every short-lived process leaked one slot for good.

modes.text: counts free and zombie slots
starts 4 processes that end at once, waits 0.2 s, compares free slots before and after
waits for the reaper and counts what it freed

security.tryIt:
seclab attack zombie_leak live
ps                               # no "leak" zombies left

defence.fix: free zombie slots and stacks on every timer tick
defence.called: scheduler_tick() (core/scheduler) on every timer tick, and by `seclab repair`.
defence.rules:
1. only zombies are freed
2. never the running process: we are standing on its stack
defence.why: a process cannot free its own stack while it runs on it, so process_exit() only marks it ZOMBIE. Someone else must free it later, from a different stack. That someone is the reaper.

syscalls.name: sbrk
syscalls.summary: move the "program break", the end of the heap.
syscalls.details:
USER_BRK_START            break                     USER_BRK_END
       |=========== heap ===========|      free...       |

sbrk(+n) moves the break up by n bytes and maps any new pages it now
covers; sbrk(-n) moves it down and unmaps whole pages it left. It
returns the OLD break, so sbrk(n) == "here are your n new bytes".
malloc() in a C library is built on top of exactly this.

For now there is one break for the whole system, because all processes
share one address space.
syscalls.uses: umem_map / umem_unmap (core/umem), cpu_irq_save (arch/x86/cpu), rlimit_data_ok (cpu_management/core/rlimit): RLIMIT_DATA caps the heap size of the caller.

syscalls.name: mmap
syscalls.summary: map a new region of zeroed pages for the caller.
syscalls.details:
Real mmap() also maps files and takes protection flags. UzOS keeps
the core idea: "give me N bytes of fresh memory, you pick where".
The region goes in the mmap area (MMAP_START..MMAP_END) and is
recorded, so only munmap() of exactly this region can remove it.
syscalls.uses: umem_region_add + umem_map (core/umem), and the defence mmap_page_count to turn 'length' into pages safely.

syscalls.name: munmap
syscalls.summary: unmap a region and free its frames.
syscalls.details:
Only a region that mmap() handed out, as a whole, can be unmapped.
Without that rule, munmap(<kernel address>) would free frames the
kernel is still using.
syscalls.uses: umem_unmap + umem_region_remove (core/umem), and the defences mmap_page_count and mmap_ownership.

security.what: kfree a block twice, a pointer into a block, or a non-heap address
security.story: `kfree(p)` finds the block header 16 bytes **before** `p` and writes to it. So it goes wrong when `p` is not what `kmalloc()` returned.

modes.text: lists the three bad frees
allocates two blocks, does the three bad frees for real, frees the blocks properly, then checks the heap is healthy

security.tryIt:
seclab attack heap_double_free live
heapinfo

defence.fix: kfree only accepts real, in-use heap blocks
defence.called: kfree() (core/kheap), before the block is touched.
defence.rules:
1. p lies inside the heap, where a block's data can start
2. p is 8-byte aligned, like every block kmalloc() returns
3. the header just before p has the heap magic
4. the block is in use (not already freed)
defence.why: kfree() writes into the header just before p. With a pointer from outside the heap, it would write into random memory; with a double free, the block's list could end up linked twice. Rule 1 and 2 are checked first, so a bad pointer is never even read through.

security.what: writing past a block's end overwrites the next block's header
security.story: ``` [hdr A| data A: 16 bytes ][hdr B: magic size is_free next| data B ] ^-- byte 16 of A is byte 0 of B's header ```

modes.text: explains where A ends and B begins
with interrupts off, really writes 20 bytes into A, shows heapinfo reporting CORRUPTED, calls kfree(A) so the canary check meets B, then restores B's header exactly

security.tryIt:
seclab attack heap_overflow live
audit
heapinfo                         # Health: OK

defence.fix: check each heap header's magic before following it
defence.called: kmalloc() and kfree() (core/kheap), for every header before they follow its 'next' pointer.
defence.rules:
1. the header holds KHEAP_MAGIC (the "canary")
2. 'next' is NULL, or points further on inside the heap
defence.why: writing past the end of a block lands in the next block's header. Its 'next' pointer would then send the heap code into random memory. The magic number works like a canary in a coal mine: if it is gone, something overwrote the header, so we stop walking instead of following garbage. kmalloc() then fails cleanly instead of crashing.

security.what: a huge mmap length rounds to 0 pages and maps nothing
security.story: `mmap(length)` must turn bytes into whole pages. The usual formula is

modes.text: shows the naive formula giving 0 pages
calls the real sys_mmap() with 0xFFFFFFFF, 0 and 16 MiB + 1 (all must fail), then with 4096 (must work)

security.tryIt:

seclab attack mmap_length_wrap live

defence.fix: limit mmap length and round it to pages without overflow
defence.called: sys_mmap() and sys_munmap() (syscalls/), before anything else.
defence.rules:
1. 0 < length <= MMAP_MAX_BYTES
2. pages = length / PAGE_SIZE, + 1 if there is a remainder
defence.why: the usual "(length + PAGE_SIZE - 1) / PAGE_SIZE" overflows for a length near 4 GiB and gives 0 pages: mmap would "succeed" with no memory behind it. Rule 2 has no addition that can overflow, and rule 1 stops one call from asking for all of RAM.

security.what: munmap kernel memory so its frames get freed and reused
security.story: `munmap(addr, length)` unmaps pages **and frees their frames**. The old version checked only that `addr` was below `0xC0000000`, which in UzOS includes the kernel. So

modes.text: lists the targets
calls the real sys_munmap() on the kernel code, the kernel heap, and half of a fresh mmap region (all must be refused, with no frame freed), then unmaps the whole region (allowed)

defence.fix: munmap only exact regions that mmap handed out
defence.called: sys_munmap() (syscalls/munmap), before anything is unmapped.
defence.why: munmap() frees the frames behind the pages. If any address were accepted, munmap(0x100000, 4096) would free the frame holding the kernel's own code, and the next allocation would overwrite it. Only memory you got from mmap() is yours to give back.

security.what: a NULL pointer access silently uses the memory at address 0
security.story: ```c struct thing *p = NULL;     // forgot to set it p->count = 5;               // writes to address 0 + offset ```

the same check, with a verdict

defence.fix: keep page 0 unmapped so NULL pointer accesses fault
defence.called: vmm_init() (core/vmm), while building the page tables.
defence.why: the first 8 MiB are identity mapped for the kernel. Without this, page 0 is mapped too, and a NULL pointer access silently reads or overwrites the BIOS's interrupt table at address 0. The bug goes unnoticed. With page 0 unmapped, the same bug stops at once with a page fault that names the address.

security.what: free a kernel frame, a bogus address, or a frame twice
security.story: The PMM gives the most recently freed frames to the next caller. So.

modes.text: lists the four bad frees
calls the real pmm_free_block() with each one (including a real double free) and checks the used-frame count does not move

security.tryIt:
seclab attack pmm_bad_free live
audit

defence.fix: free only aligned, real, non-reserved frames that are in use
defence.called: pmm_free_block() (core/pmm), before the bitmap is touched.
defence.rules:
1. the address is the start of a frame (multiple of 4096)
2. the frame is real RAM (inside the bitmap's range)
3. the frame is not reserved (kernel image, firmware, boot data)
4. the frame is in use (freeing a free frame = double free)
defence.why: a freed frame is handed to the next pmm_alloc_block() caller. Freeing a kernel frame means the kernel's own code gets overwritten; a double free hands one frame to two owners.

security.what: an address range wraps past 4 GiB or points into the kernel
security.story: A system call gets an address range `(start, size)` from a program. The obvious check is `start + size <= END`. But in 32 bits.

modes.text: runs the naive check on five crafted ranges (one is an unmapped user page) and shows which it lets through
offers the same ranges to def_user_range_ok(); all must be refused

security.tryIt:
seclab attack user_ptr_wrap          # see the naive check fail
seclab attack user_ptr_wrap live

defence.fix: ring 3 pointers must be inside user space and mapped, without wrap
defence.called: the int 0x80 handler (process_management), for every address a ring 3 program passes in: buffers (read, write, getcwd, munmap) and strings (paths for open, mkdir, ...).
defence.rules:
1. the whole range is inside user space
(USER_SPACE_START <= start, size <= USER_SPACE_END - start)
2. every page in it is mapped, with the USER bit
A string is checked byte by byte the same way, up to its NUL.
defence.why: "start + size" in 32 bits wraps: 0xFFFFFFF0 + 0x20 = 0x10, so a naive check passes a range that covers the kernel. And if a page is not mapped, the KERNEL page-faults while copying, which halts the whole OS. A program must only ever make itself fail.

commands.summary: call every CPU syscall from ring 3, check each answer.

honest test is a user program: cpucalls.s runs in ring 3 as user 1
(guest), goes through all of them with int 0x80 (the [syscall] trace
shows each one), and leaves every answer in the usertask mailbox.
This command then prints them next to what a correct kernel answers:

nice, use SCHED_FIFO, raise a hard limit, or ask for a CPU or NUMA
node that does not exist. The last part makes two real threads with
clone() and clone3(), which report their own ids and end with exit();
exit_group() then ends the program.

How: read the tick counters (the same as /proc/stat), wait, read
again; the differences are the CPU use of that interval. %iowait,
%irq, %soft and %steal stay 0: UzOS has no disks to wait for, does
not count interrupt time apart, and is not a hypervisor guest that
could be stolen from... as far as it can tell.
Ctrl+C stops it.
commands.uses: cpu_account_totals (core/accounting), affinity_cpu_count (core/affinity), sys_sleep_interruptible (process_management), rtc_read (device_management), ui_* (ui), arg_next / atoi / strcmp (lib).

commands.name: nice
commands.summary: start a command with a different nice.
commands.details:
nice                   print the niceness of the shell (0)
  nice ls                ls with nice 10 (the default step)
  nice -n 5 spawn        spawn with nice 5: the worker inherits it
  nice -n -10 top        top with nice -10: only root may go below 0
  nice -5 ls             old syntax for -n 5

The command runs as a NEW process (run_child.c, this folder) whose nice is changed
before it may run; the shell itself stays at its own nice. If the
change is refused (a user asking for less than 0), the command still
runs, unchanged, after a warning: that is what Linux's nice does.
commands.uses: nice_run_child (run_child.c, this folder), priority_set_nice / NICE_* (core/priority), the current process (process_management), ui_* (ui), arg_next / atoi / strcmp (lib).

commands.name: nproc
commands.summary: how many CPUs may I use?
commands.details:
nproc              CPUs in the caller's affinity mask (what a program
                   should use for "how many worker threads?")
nproc --all        CPUs the system has, whatever the mask says
nproc --ignore=N   N fewer (but never less than 1)
commands.uses: affinity_get / affinity_cpu_count (core/affinity), the current process (process_management), ui_* (ui), atoi / strncmp (lib).

commands.name: numactl
commands.summary: NUMA nodes, and run a command placed on them.
commands.details:
numactl --hardware   (-H)    the nodes: CPUs, memory, distances
  numactl --show       (-s)    the shell's memory policy and CPUs

  numactl [options] command    run it with a placement:
    --membind=NODES     -m     memory only from these nodes   (MPOL_BIND)
    --preferred=NODE    -p     memory from here first         (MPOL_PREFERRED)
    --interleave=NODES  -i     memory spread over the nodes   (MPOL_INTERLEAVE)
    --localalloc        -l     memory of the CPU's own node   (MPOL_LOCAL)
    --cpunodebind=NODES -N     only the CPUs of these nodes   (affinity)
    --physcpubind=CPUS  -C     only these CPUs                (affinity)
  NODES / CPUS: "0", "0-1", "0,1" or "all".

UzOS has one node (core/numa), so node 0 is the only one that works;
asking for node 1 is refused, as on a machine without a node 1.

commands.name: perf
commands.summary: one command, several tools.
commands.details:
perf stat command      count what a command did     (perf_stat/)
  perf record command    sample where time goes        (perf_record/)
  perf report            show what record found        (perf_report/)
  perf list              the events UzOS can count     (here)

This file only reads the first word and hands the rest of the line
to the tool, as Linux's perf does.
commands.uses: cmd_perf_stat / cmd_perf_record / cmd_perf_report (their folders), ui_* (ui), arg_next / strcmp (lib).

commands.name: perf record
commands.summary: where does the CPU spend its time?
commands.details:
perf record ls                   sample while ls runs -> ./perf.data
  perf record -o run1.data spawn   write to another file
  perf report                      look at the result (perf_report/)

While the command runs, every timer tick (100 a second) the kernel
notes which process was on the CPU, in which ring, and at which
instruction (EIP): core/perf. Like Linux's `perf record -a`, the
samples cover the whole system, so you also see what ran BESIDES your
command (the idle task, statusd...). Afterwards the samples are
written to a file with the normal file syscalls.

  [ perf record: Woken up 1 times to write data ]
  [ perf record: Captured and wrote 0.008 MB perf.data (412 samples) ]

commands.name: perf report
commands.summary: which functions used the CPU?
commands.details:
# Samples: 412 of event 'cpu-clock' (timer tick, 100 Hz)
  # Overhead  Command       Shared Object  Symbol
      91.26%  idle          [kernel]       [k] power_idle
       4.13%  kernel_main   [kernel]       [k] vga_put_char
       1.21%  spin          spin           [.] 0x40000004

  perf report                  read ./perf.data
  perf report -i run1.data     another file
  perf report --sort comm      by process only

Each sample is an EIP. For kernel code (ring 0, "[k]") the kernel's
own symbol table (ksyms.c, in this folder) turns it into a function name; ring 3
programs ("[.]") have no symbols in UzOS, so their address is shown.
Overhead = the share of all samples that fell into that function:
where the time went.
commands.uses: perf_file_header_t / perf_sample_t (core/perf), ksyms_lookup (ksyms.c, this folder), sys_open / sys_read / sys_close (io_management), def_safe_text (ui defence safe_text), ui_* (ui), arg_next / format / string (lib).

commands.name: perf stat
commands.summary: run it, then count what it did.
commands.details:
Performance counter stats for 'ls':

             12.34 msec task-clock         #    0.410 CPUs utilized
                 3      context-switches   #  243.112 /sec
                 0      cpu-migrations     #    0.000 /sec
                 0      page-faults        #    0.000 /sec
        33,145,021      cycles             #    2.686 GHz
   <not supported>      instructions

       0.030102345 seconds time elapsed

task-clock and cycles are EXACT: the cycle counter is read on every
task switch (core/accounting), so they count only the time the
command really had the CPU. "CPUs utilized" = task-clock / elapsed:
below 1 means it also waited. The command runs as its own process
(run_child.c, this folder); processes it starts are counted too.
instructions needs a hardware PMU, which UzOS does not drive.
commands.uses: perf_stat_run_child (run_child.c, this folder), tsc_mhz / tsc_cycles_to_us (core/tsc), timer_frequency (device_management), ui_* (ui).

commands.name: pidstat
commands.summary: CPU use per process, per interval.
commands.details:
Time        UID    PID   %usr %system  %wait   %CPU  CPU  Command
  19:19:04      0      2   0.00    3.00   0.00   3.00    0  kernel_main

  pidstat              since each process started
  pidstat 1 5          every second, five times, then the average
  pidstat -p 7 1       only PID 7
  pidstat -w 1         context switches instead:
                         cswch/s    voluntary (it slept, waited)
                         nvcswch/s  involuntary (preempted)

%wait is the time a process was READY but another one had the CPU:
it wanted to run and could not. High %wait = the CPU is too busy.

With an interval only processes that used the CPU in it are shown
(like Linux). Ctrl+C stops it.
commands.uses: the process table (process_management), affinity_current_cpu (core/affinity), timer_* / rtc_read (device_management), sys_sleep_interruptible, def_safe_text (ui defence safe_text), ui_* (ui), arg_next / atoi / strcmp (lib).

commands.name: powerprofilesctl
commands.summary: fast, balanced or frugal?
commands.details:
powerprofilesctl list           the three profiles, '*' = the active one
  powerprofilesctl get            the active profile's name
  powerprofilesctl set NAME       switch (performance, balanced, power-saver)

What each profile really changes in UzOS is in core/power: how the
idle CPU waits (spin or hlt) and how long one turn on the CPU lasts.
Like on Linux, any logged-in user may switch.
commands.uses: power_* (core/power), ui_* (ui), arg_next / strcmp (lib).

commands.name: ps
commands.summary: a snapshot of the processes.
commands.details:
ps                  your processes:             PID TTY TIME CMD
  ps -e   (or -A)     every process
  ps -f               full: UID PID PPID C STIME TTY TIME CMD
  ps -L               one row per THREAD, with its LWP (thread id)
  ps aux              BSD style: USER PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS TTY STAT START TIME COMMAND
  ps -eo pid,comm,%cpu            choose the columns (ps -o help lists them)
  ps -p 7,8   ps -u guest         only these processes / this user's
  ps -e --sort=-%cpu              sorted, '-' = biggest first

Without -L, ps shows one row per process: a thread group's other
threads (clone(CLONE_THREAD)) are hidden behind their leader.
Names go through def_safe_text, so a process name can never break the
table (the ui defence safe_text, attack output_spoof).

commands.name: renice
commands.summary: change the nice value of running processes.
commands.details:
renice 10 -p 7 8        processes 7 and 8 get nice 10
  renice -n 5 -p 7        the same with -n
  renice 19 -u guest      every process of user guest

For each one it prints what changed, as Linux does:

  7 (process ID) old priority 0, new priority 10

The rules are the defence priority_bounds (via setpriority): users may
only renice their own processes, and only upward (nicer).

commands.name: sar
commands.summary: System Activity Reporter.
commands.details:
sar               the last minute, from the kernel's own history
                  (one line per 10 seconds; Linux's sar reads a log
                  its collector wrote every 10 minutes)
sar 1 5           live: every second, five times, then the average
sar -u ...        CPU use (the default)
sar -q ...        run queue: runq-sz, plist-sz, load averages
sar -w ...        task creation and context switches per second

Time        CPU     %user     %nice   %system   %iowait    %steal     %idle
19:19:04    all      0.00      0.00      3.00      0.00      0.00     97.00
commands.uses: cpu_history / cpu_account_* (core/accounting), loadavg_* (core/loadavg), cpu_task_forks (core/task), the process table (process_management), timer_* / rtc_read (device_management), sys_sleep_interruptible, ui_* (ui), arg_next / atoi / strcmp (lib).

commands.name: systemctl
commands.summary: the services, and their resource settings.
commands.details:
systemctl                    list the units (= list-units)
  systemctl status statusd     one service: state, PID, CPU used, policy
  systemctl show statusd       its settings as Name=value lines

On Linux, systemd starts the services and keeps one "unit" for each.
UzOS's services are its SYSTEM processes (process_t.is_system): the
idle task, kernel_main (the shell) and statusd (the status bar). Each
one is shown as <name>.service. The resource settings (Nice,
CPUSchedulingPolicy, CPUAffinity, Limit*) are the real values from
the process table, under the names systemd uses for them.

Starting and stopping is not offered: system processes cannot be
killed (kill_guard) and are started by the kernel itself.

commands.name: systemd cgtop
commands.summary: CPU and memory per group of processes.
commands.details:
Control Group                          Tasks    %CPU     Memory
  /                                          6     4.0      24.0K
  /system.slice                              2     4.0       8.0K
  /user.slice                                3     0.0      12.0K
  /user.slice/user-0.slice                   2     0.0       8.0K
  /user.slice/user-1000.slice                1     0.0       4.0K

Linux puts every process in a CONTROL GROUP (cgroup), a tree: services
under /system.slice, each user's login under /user.slice/user-UID.slice.
Limits and accounting then apply to a whole group at once.

UzOS has no cgroups, but the same grouping can be computed: system
processes (is_system) form /system.slice, every other process belongs
to its user's slice. The idle task is not counted (idle is not use).
Memory = each process's 4 KiB kernel stack.

  systemd-cgtop          live, full screen, every second; q quits
  systemd-cgtop -n 2     print twice to the console, then stop
commands.uses: the process table and the idle task (process_management), vga_* / keyboard_pop_key / timer (device_management), sys_sleep_interruptible, ui_* (ui), format / arg_next / atoi (lib).

commands.name: taskset
commands.summary: which CPUs a process may run on.
commands.details:
taskset -p 7               pid 7's current affinity mask: 1
  taskset -cp 7              pid 7's current affinity list: 0
  taskset -p 1 7             set the mask of 7 to 0x1 (CPU 0)
  taskset -c -p 0 7          the same, as a CPU list
  taskset 1 ls               run ls on the CPUs of mask 0x1
  taskset -c 0 ls            run ls on CPU 0

Masks are hexadecimal (bit n = CPU n), lists are "0", "0-3", "0,2".
With one CPU the only valid choice is CPU 0; asking for CPU 1 is
refused, as on a real machine without a CPU 1.
commands.uses: affinity_* (core/affinity), taskset_run_child (run_child.c, this folder), the process table (process_management), ui_* (ui), arg_next / strtoul / strcmp (lib).

commands.name: time
commands.summary: how long it took, and whose time it was.
commands.details:
$ time ls
  ...output of ls...

  real    0m0.031s       wall clock: from start to end
  user    0m0.000s       CPU time in ring 3 (the program itself)
  sys     0m0.030s       CPU time in ring 0 (the kernel, for it)

real > user + sys: the command waited (slept, or other processes ran).
real < user + sys can only happen with several CPUs.

Shell commands are kernel code, so their time is "sys"; a ring 3
program (exec, seclab ... live) shows "user" time too. The command
runs as its own process (run_child.c, this folder); its usage record, including
any processes it started, comes from core/task.

user and sys are counted in timer ticks (10 ms each); real is
measured with the TSC, to the microsecond.
commands.uses: time_run_child (run_child.c, this folder), tsc_cycles_to_us (core/tsc), timer_frequency (device_management), ui_* (ui).

commands.name: top
commands.summary: a live, full-screen view of the CPU and the processes.
commands.details:
top - 19:19:03 up 5 min,  1 user,  load average: 0.00, 0.01, 0.05
  Tasks:   6 total,   1 running,   5 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
  %Cpu(s):  1.0 us,  3.0 sy,  0.0 ni, 96.0 id,  0.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si,  0.0 st
  MiB Mem :    127.0 total,    118.2 free,      8.8 used,      0.0 buff/cache
  MiB Swap:      0.0 total,      0.0 free,      0.0 used.    118.2 avail Mem

      PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES  S  %CPU  %MEM      TIME+ COMMAND
        2 root      20   0       4      4  R   3.0   0.0    0:00.31 kernel_main

  keys:  q quit   P sort by CPU   N by PID   T by CPU time   1 per-CPU line
  top -b -n 2      batch: print twice to the console, no full screen
  top -d 2         refresh every 2 s (default 3)
  top -p 7         only PID 7

PR is the kernel's priority: 20 + nice for normal processes, "rt" or
-1 - rt_priority for real-time ones. The CPU line is the last full
second of core/accounting.

While top runs the shell is not reading the keyboard (it is busy
running us), so top reads the keys itself. It borrows the whole
screen (vga_fullscreen); when it quits the old screen comes back.
commands.uses: cpu_load (core/accounting), loadavg_* (core/loadavg), policy_is_realtime (core/policy), the process table (process_management), pmm_* (memory_management), users_name (user_management), timer_* / rtc_read / vga_* / keyboard_pop_key (device_management), sys_sleep_interruptible (process_management), def_safe_text (ui defence safe_text), format / string (lib).

commands.name: turbostat
commands.summary: clock, busy time and idle per interval.
commands.details:
Core  CPU  Avg_MHz  Busy%  Bzy_MHz  TSC_MHz     IRQ    POLL%     C1%
     -    -       80   3.00        -     2686     102     0.00   97.00
     0    0       80   3.00        -     2686     102     0.00   97.00

  Avg_MHz   cycles really spent working per second = Busy% x TSC_MHz
  Busy%     time not in the idle task
  Bzy_MHz   the clock WHILE busy: needs the APERF/MPERF counters of a
            real CPU (QEMU has none): "-"
  TSC_MHz   the cycle counter's rate (core/tsc)
  IRQ       interrupts in the interval
  POLL% C1% idle time by idle state (core/power: spin or hlt)

  turbostat              every 5 s until Ctrl+C (Linux's default)
  turbostat -i 1 -n 3    every second, three times

Linux's turbostat reads model-specific registers (MSRs) and so needs
root; UzOS computes everything from its own counters.
