commands.name: ulimit
commands.summary: the shell's own resource limits.
commands.details:
ulimit             the file size limit (bash shows this one alone)
  ulimit -a          every limit UzOS uses, with its letter
  ulimit -t          one limit (soft): -t cpu  -f fsize  -d data
                     -s stack  -u nproc  -n nofile  -e nice  -r rtprio
  ulimit -t 2        set it (soft AND hard, like bash)
  ulimit -S -t 2     only the soft limit;  -H: only the hard limit
  ulimit -t unlimited

Like in bash it is a SHELL setting: it changes the limits of the
shell's process (kernel_main), and every command started from now on
inherits them (core/task). Raising a hard limit needs root
(CAP_RESOURCE); anyone may lower one, and then cannot raise it back.
commands.uses: rlimit_* (core/rlimit), the current process (process_management), ui_* (ui), arg_next / strtoul / strcmp (lib).

commands.name: uptime
commands.summary: time, uptime, users, load average.
commands.details:
19:19:03 up 5 min,  1 user,  load average: 0.00, 0.01, 0.05

  uptime -p     "up 5 minutes" (pretty)
  uptime -s     when the system started: "2026-10-26 19:14:00"

The three load averages (1, 5, 15 minutes) say how many processes
wanted the CPU on average: see core/loadavg. "1 user": UzOS has one
console, so one logged-in session.
commands.uses: loadavg_get / loadavg_format (core/loadavg), timer_uptime_ms (device_management/timer), rtc_read / rtc_unix_time (device_management/rtc), ui_* (ui), strcmp (lib/string).

commands.name: vmstat
commands.summary: the whole system in one line.
commands.details:
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- ---io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
   r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so   bi   bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
   1  0      0 120712      0      0    0    0    0    0  101   24  0  2 98  0  0

  r      processes that want the CPU (READY or RUNNING)
  b      processes blocked on I/O (UzOS: none, nothing waits for a disk)
  free   free memory in KiB
  in     interrupts per second       cs   context switches per second
  us sy id   user, system, idle % of the CPU

The first line is the average since boot (as in Linux); with an
interval, every next line covers that interval. Ctrl+C stops it.

syscalls.name: getpid
syscalls.summary: return the process ID of the caller.
syscalls.details:
A "process" in Linux terms is a thread GROUP: the first thread and
every thread it made with clone(CLONE_THREAD). They all answer the
same getpid(), the group's id (tgid). A process without threads is a
group of one, so its tgid is simply its pid.

  thread          pid (gettid)    tgid (getpid)
  main            7               7
  clone()d        8               7

syscalls.name: sched_yield
syscalls.summary: give the rest of this turn to the next process.
syscalls.details:
The caller stays READY. The scheduler picks again (core/priority):
processes at the SAME rank go first (round robin), so yielding lets
your equals run; a lower-ranked process still waits. A SCHED_FIFO
process that yields goes to the back of its level, the only way it
ever lets an equal run.

syscalls.name: cputime
syscalls.summary: CPU time used, not wall-clock time.
syscalls.details:
uptime() says how long the SYSTEM has run. cputime() says how long a
PROCESS actually had the CPU. A program that sleeps 10 s uses almost
no CPU time; a busy loop uses all of it. (Like clock() / times() in C.)
syscalls.uses: cpu_account_ms (core/accounting), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management).

syscalls.name: setpriority
syscalls.summary: the Unix way to be nice.
syscalls.details:
setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, 10)      me: nice 10 (less CPU)
    setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 7, 5)       process 7: nice 5
    setpriority(PRIO_USER, 1000, 19)      every process of uid 1000

Each change goes through priority_set_nice(), where the defence
priority_bounds checks the value and the caller's rights (users may
only raise nice, on their own processes).
syscalls.uses: priority_set_nice (core/priority), the process table and the current process (process_management).

syscalls.name: getpriority
syscalls.summary: read the nice value, Linux style.
syscalls.details:
Why "20 - nice" and not the nice value itself? Nice can be -1, and -1
is also what a failed syscall returns. So the raw syscall answers
20 - nice, a number from 1 to 40 that is never negative; the C
library turns it back into the nice value. (Linux does exactly this.)

    nice -20 -> 40     nice 0 -> 20     nice 19 -> 1     error -> -1
syscalls.uses: the process table and the current process (process_management), NICE_MAX (core/priority).

syscalls.name: sched_setscheduler
syscalls.summary: policy + priority in one call.
syscalls.details:
struct sched_param p = { .sched_priority = 20 };
    sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_FIFO, &p);     // me: real-time, level 20
    sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_OTHER, &p0);   // back to normal (priority 0)

The checks (a known policy, a priority in its range, the right to
real-time) are the defence priority_bounds, inside policy_set().

syscalls.name: sched_getscheduler
syscalls.summary: read a process's policy.
syscalls.details: Reading is allowed for every process (as in Linux): it changes nothing.
syscalls.uses: SCHED_RESET_ON_FORK (core/policy), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management).

syscalls.name: sched_setparam
syscalls.summary: a new priority, the same policy.
syscalls.details:
Only real-time policies have a priority here (1..99); for SCHED_OTHER
the only valid value is 0, and the "priority" of a normal process is
its nice value (setpriority).
syscalls.uses: policy_set (core/policy), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management).

syscalls.name: sched_getparam
syscalls.summary: a process's real-time priority.
syscalls.details: 1..99 for SCHED_FIFO / SCHED_RR, 0 for every other policy.

syscalls.name: sched_get_priority_min
syscalls.summary: the bottom of a policy's range.
syscalls.details:
Programs must not guess the range ("is it 1..99 or 0..99?"): they ask.
A portable program picks e.g. min + 10 for a modest real-time priority.

syscalls.name: sched_get_priority_max
syscalls.summary: the top of a policy's range.

syscalls.name: sched_rr_get_interval
syscalls.summary: the time slice of a process.
syscalls.details:
The name says "RR" because the answer matters most for SCHED_RR: it
is how long a real-time process runs before the next one at its level
gets a turn. UzOS answers for every policy, from the same function the
scheduler uses (policy_slice_ticks), so it is never out of date:

    SCHED_RR      10 ticks = 100 ms
    SCHED_OTHER    5 ticks =  50 ms (10 in the power-saver profile)
    SCHED_FIFO     0: a FIFO turn ends only when the process sleeps
syscalls.uses: policy_slice_ticks (core/policy), timer_frequency (device_management), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management).

syscalls.name: sched_setaffinity
syscalls.summary: pin a process to CPUs.
syscalls.details:
The mask comes as bytes (Linux's cpu_set_t can be 128 bytes for 1024
CPUs). UzOS reads the first 4 bytes = CPUs 0-31; any bit set further
on names a CPU that does not exist, so the call is refused.

syscalls.name: sched_getaffinity
syscalls.summary: read a process's CPU mask.
syscalls.details:
Like Linux, the raw syscall returns how many bytes of mask it wrote,
and the rest of the caller's buffer is left alone.
syscalls.uses: affinity_get (core/affinity), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management).

syscalls.name: sched_setattr
syscalls.summary: the newest, most complete call.
syscalls.details:
sched_setscheduler() cannot set a nice value, and setpriority()
cannot set a policy. sched_setattr() takes them all at once:

    sched_attr_t a = { .size = 48, .sched_policy = SCHED_BATCH,
                       .sched_nice = 5 };
    sched_setattr(0, &a, 0);

attr->size tells which version of the struct the caller knows, so
old programs keep working when Linux adds fields. UzOS knows the
first version (48 bytes) and refuses SCHED_DEADLINE.

Both parts are checked by the defence priority_bounds (policy_set,
priority_set_nice); nothing is changed unless both are allowed.
syscalls.uses: policy_set (core/policy), priority_set_nice (core/priority), def_nice_change_allowed / def_policy_change_allowed (defence priority_bounds), the process table (process_management).

syscalls.name: sched_getattr
syscalls.summary: policy, nice, rt priority, flags.
syscalls.uses: SCHED_* (core/policy), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management), memset (lib/string).

syscalls.name: getrlimit
syscalls.summary: one limit of the caller.

syscalls.name: setrlimit
syscalls.summary: lower (or, as root, raise) one limit.
syscalls.details:
rlimit_t l = { .cur = 2, .max = 2 };
    setrlimit(RLIMIT_CPU, &l);    // after 2 s of CPU: killed

A lowered hard limit cannot be raised again without CAP_RESOURCE:
that is what makes it a real limit and not a suggestion.

syscalls.name: prlimit64
syscalls.summary: getrlimit + setrlimit for another process.
syscalls.details:
prlimit64(7, RLIMIT_CPU, &new, &old)    the `prlimit` tool's call

Two differences from setrlimit():
  - it names a process: only your own, unless you hold CAP_RESOURCE
  - the values are 64-bit ("64"), so limits above 4 GiB fit. UzOS
    keeps 32-bit limits: anything above 0xFFFFFFFE means unlimited.
syscalls.uses: rlimit_get / rlimit_set (core/rlimit), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management).

syscalls.name: getcpu
syscalls.summary: where am I running right now?
syscalls.details:
On a multi-CPU machine the answer can be out of date the moment it
returns (the scheduler may move the process). It is a hint, used for
per-CPU data. UzOS runs on CPU 0, which is on node 0.

syscalls.name: perf_event_open
syscalls.summary: a counter behind a file descriptor.
syscalls.details:
perf_event_attr_t a = { PERF_TYPE_SOFTWARE, sizeof(a),
                            PERF_COUNT_SW_CONTEXT_SWITCHES };
    int fd = perf_event_open(&a, 0, -1, -1, 0);
    ...
    uint64_t n; read(fd, &n, 8);     // switches since the open
    close(fd);

Who may watch whom:
  pid 0 / your own process   anyone
  another user's process     CAP_PRIORITY (root)
  pid -1 (the whole system)  CAP_PRIORITY (root)
(Linux uses perf_event_paranoid and CAP_PERFMON for this.)
syscalls.uses: perf_counter_create (perf_counter.c, this folder), fd_alloc / fd_release (io_management), rlimit_nofile (core/rlimit), caps_has (security_management), the current process (process_management).

syscalls.name: gettid
syscalls.summary: the id of this one thread.
syscalls.details:
getpid()   the PROCESS (thread group): the same for all its threads
  gettid()   the THREAD: different for each

In UzOS every thread is a slot in the process table, so a thread's id
is simply its pid there. For the first thread of a group the two
answers are equal (tid == tgid).

syscalls.name: clone
syscalls.summary: one call, two returns.
syscalls.details:
tid = clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_SIGHAND | CLONE_THREAD, stack_top, ...);
    if (tid == 0)   -> I am the new thread, on stack_top
    else            -> I am the parent, tid is the new thread

How the child gets there:

  parent (ring 3)                        child
  int 0x80 (clone)
    copy the parent's saved registers, change two:
        eax = 0 (so the child knows it is the child)
        esp = 'stack'
    process_create(..., thread_start)
  parent returns with eax = child id     thread_start() in ring 0
                                         clone_enter_user(copy) -> iret
                                         -> ring 3, after int 0x80, eax 0

A thread is a normal UzOS process (a slot, a pid, a kernel stack); it
only shares the memory, which every process does in UzOS today.
syscalls.uses: process_create / process_get_by_pid / the process table and the current process (process_management), vfs_open (filesystem_management) for the copied files, cpu_irq_save (arch/x86/cpu), clone_enter_user (clone_enter.s, this folder).

syscalls.name: clone3
syscalls.summary: the extensible clone().
syscalls.details:
clone() ran out of registers and flag bits. clone3() takes ONE
pointer to a struct plus its size; new fields can be added at the
end, and the size tells the kernel which version the program knows.

Two things differ from clone():
  - the stack is given as (lowest address, size), not as its top
  - the exit signal has its own field instead of the flags' low byte

The child is made exactly as clone() makes it (this file has its own
copy of that code): a new process starts in ring 0 at thread_start()
and "returns" to ring 3 with a copy of the parent's registers,
EAX = 0 and ESP = the top of the new stack (clone3_enter.s).
syscalls.uses: process_create / process_get_by_pid / the process table and the current process (process_management), vfs_open (filesystem_management), cpu_irq_save (arch/x86/cpu), clone3_enter_user (clone3_enter.s, this folder).

syscalls.name: move_pages
syscalls.summary: ask about (or move) single pages.
syscalls.details:
void *pages[1] = { buffer };
    int status[1];
    move_pages(0, 1, pages, NULL, status, 0);   // status[0] = node of buffer

With one node every mapped page is already on node 0: "moving" it to
node 0 succeeds with nothing to do, moving it anywhere else fails
with ENODEV for that page. The answers are still real: an unmapped
address really is reported as ENOENT.
syscalls.uses: numa_node_of_address / numa_online_nodes (core/numa), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management), caps_has (security_management) for other users' processes.

syscalls.name: mbind
syscalls.summary: "this buffer should live on node 1".
syscalls.details:
set_mempolicy() sets a policy for all of a process's memory; mbind()
sets one for a single range, e.g. a big array that one CPU group
works on. Rules (as in Linux):
  - addr is page aligned, the range is mapped user memory
  - mode and nodes form a valid policy (core/numa)
  - MPOL_MF_STRICT: fail if a page is already on a node outside the
    mask (never happens with one node)
  - MPOL_MF_MOVE: move such pages (none to move with one node)
UzOS remembers up to 4 ranges per process; get_mempolicy(MPOL_F_ADDR)
reads them back.

syscalls.name: set_mempolicy
syscalls.summary: the process's memory policy.
syscalls.details:
uint32_t nodes = 1 << 0;
    set_mempolicy(MPOL_BIND, &nodes, 32);   // only node 0
    set_mempolicy(MPOL_DEFAULT, NULL, 0);   // back to the default

Children inherit it (core/task). It is what `numactl --membind=0`
sets before starting a program.

syscalls.name: get_mempolicy
syscalls.summary: four questions in one call.
syscalls.details:
get_mempolicy(&mode, &nodes, 32, 0, 0)                   my policy
get_mempolicy(&mode, &nodes, 32, buf, MPOL_F_ADDR)       policy of buf (mbind)
get_mempolicy(&node, 0, 0, buf, MPOL_F_NODE|MPOL_F_ADDR) node of buf's page
get_mempolicy(0, &nodes, 32, 0, MPOL_F_MEMS_ALLOWED)     nodes I may use

syscalls.name: migrate_pages
syscalls.summary: a whole process moves house.
syscalls.details:
Used when a program is moved to CPUs of another node: its memory
should follow it. With one node, old and new must both be node 0,
so every page is already where it belongs and the answer is 0 (no
page failed). Masks naming a node that does not exist are refused.
syscalls.uses: numa_online_nodes (core/numa), process_get_by_pid and the current process (process_management), caps_has (security_management).

syscalls.name: membarrier
syscalls.summary: make every thread see my writes.
syscalls.details:
CPUs may reorder memory accesses. Threads that share data put a
BARRIER between their accesses ("everything before is visible before
anything after"). membarrier() lets ONE thread do it for ALL: after
it returns, every other running thread has passed a barrier too. That
makes the fast path of the other threads cheaper (no barrier there).

How the kernel keeps the promise:
  many CPUs   interrupt every CPU running a thread of this process,
              each runs a barrier in the interrupt (expedited), or wait
              until every CPU has switched tasks once (global)
  UzOS        one CPU: every OTHER thread is not running right now,
              and a task switch is itself a full barrier. So one
              barrier here, on this CPU, is enough.

PRIVATE_EXPEDITED must be registered first (REGISTER_PRIVATE_EXPEDITED),
as in Linux; unregistered use fails.

syscalls.name: exit_group
syscalls.summary: the end of a whole program.
syscalls.details:
exit()         ends only the calling THREAD; the others go on
  exit_group()   ends every thread of the group (same getpid())

The C library's exit() really calls exit_group(): when main()
returns, all threads must stop, or the program would keep running
without its main thread.

How: kill every other process with our thread group id (tgid), then
end ourselves. process_kill() checks kill_guard: they are our own
threads, so it allows it.
syscalls.uses: process_kill / process_exit / the process table and the current process (process_management).

security.what: mis-train the predictor to steer speculation (illustration)
security.story: Train the CPU's branch predictor to guess wrong so a victim speculatively runs a path that touches a secret, then read it from the cache (Spectre v2's technique). It needs a shared, trainable predictor and out-of-order execution; UzOS has neither.

defence.fix: isolation bounds the leak; the real fix is microcode + retpolines
defence.called: nothing new at runtime: the real fixes (IBRS/IBPB microcode, retpoline compilation) live in the CPU and the compiler. What UzOS provides is the isolation that bounds the leak (core/vmm).
defence.why: honesty - a teaching kernel cannot add microcode, so the lesson is WHERE the fix lives and what isolation still buys.
defence.story: The structural fixes are **hardware and toolchain** - microcode (IBRS/IBPB) and retpolines - not something a teaching kernel can add. What UzOS provides is the isolation that bounds any leak: one task at a time, kernel pages hidden from ring 3. The lesson is where the real fix lives.

security.what: read secrets from cache hit/miss timing (illustration)
security.story: A cached byte loads far faster than one from RAM. Timing accesses reveals which addresses a victim touched, leaking secrets. It needs a fine clock.

defence.fix: ring 3 rdtsc is trapped; the tick is too coarse to time a cache
defence.called: the same CR4.TSD trap as side_channel's tsc_restrict: rdtsc in ring 3 faults (def_tsc_restrict_enable, core/tsc). Without rdtsc, ring 3's finest clock is the timer tick (10 ms).
defence.why: cache attacks (Flush+Reload, Prime+Probe) all rest on a fine clock. Take the clock away and the side channel goes quiet.
defence.story: UzOS traps ring 3 `rdtsc` (CR4.TSD, shared with side_channel), so a ring 3 attacker's finest clock is the 10 ms timer tick - millions of cycles, far too coarse to tell a cache hit (~50 cycles) from a miss (~250). No clock, no channel.

security.what: run bytes written as data by jumping into them (concept)
security.story: Write machine code into a data area you control (a buffer, the stack), then trick the program into jumping to it - your bytes run with the victim's rights.

defence.fix: concept: NX data pages stop injected code; UzOS paging has no NX bit
defence.called: nothing: the no-execute bit is a CPU feature UzOS's 32-bit paging (no PAE) does not provide, so a page cannot be marked non-executable here.
defence.why: honesty - without an NX bit UzOS cannot enforce this. The lesson is the rule and why this kernel cannot apply it; see also wx_and_aslr (ROP), the no-injection cousin of this one.
defence.story: NX / W^X: data pages are non-executable, so the jump faults and injected bytes become a crash, not code. **UzOS cannot mark a page non-executable** (32-bit paging without PAE has no NX bit), so this is a concept. Its code-reuse cousin, which needs no injection at all, is `return_oriented_programming`.

security.what: a never-sleeping loop takes a whole CPU for itself
security.story: A process that never sleeps uses a whole CPU second every second. A runaway or hostile loop keeps the CPU from everything else.

defence.fix: RLIMIT_CPU (ulimit -t): over the soft limit, the timer kills it
defence.called: the timer tick, through rlimit_check_cpu() (core/rlimit), once a second for every process.
defence.why: a runaway or hostile loop would hold the CPU for good; the limit makes it stop on its own, without anyone watching.
defence.story: RLIMIT_CPU (`ulimit -t N`) gives a process N CPU seconds; the timer tick checks the total through `rlimit_check_cpu()` and kills it once it is over. A child inherits the limit, so setting it in the shell caps every command started afterwards.

security.what: monopolise the CPU so the shell and servers never run
security.story: Keep the CPU so busy that the shell and servers never run - a denial of service from inside one machine.

defence.fix: aging + round robin: a waiting process is always served in the end
defence.called: the scheduler, on every decision, through aging (priority_effective -> def_aging_effective, core/priority).
defence.why: "denial of service" on one machine means hogging the CPU so real work never runs. Aging + round robin put a ceiling on how long anything can be kept waiting.
defence.story: Aging (security/starvation) raises a waiting process one level per 100 ms until it ties the busiest task; the round robin then gives it a turn. The scheduler calls this on every decision, so the longest waiter is always served in the end.

security.what: many machines flood one service (concept: UzOS has no network)
security.story: Many machines flood one service until its CPU or network can no longer serve real users. It needs a network and many attackers - UzOS has neither, so it cannot be a target and nothing is launched.

defence.fix: concept: no network stack = no remote flood; edge rate-limits a real one
defence.called: nothing in UzOS: there is no network stack, so there is no remote flood to meet. On a real server the defence is rate limiting, load balancing and upstream traffic filtering.
defence.why: honesty - a DDoS needs many machines and a network; UzOS is one machine with no network, so it cannot be a target. The single-machine case (hogging the CPU) is denial_of_service.
defence.story: On a real server: rate limiting per source, load balancing, and traffic filtering upstream, so the flood is dropped before it reaches the CPU. The single-machine version (one process hogging the CPU) is the `denial_of_service` pair, which is real here.

security.what: fork() in a loop to fill the process table for everyone
security.story: `while (1) fork();` doubles processes until the table is full and nothing - not even root - can start.

defence.fix: RLIMIT_NPROC (ulimit -u): a user's N-th extra fork is refused
defence.called: process_create (process_management), through rlimit_nproc_ok() (core/rlimit), on every new process.
defence.why: `while (1) fork();` doubles processes until the table is full and the machine cannot start anything, root included. A per-user cap means a bomb fills only that user's quota.
defence.story: RLIMIT_NPROC (`ulimit -u`) caps how many processes one *user* may own at once; `process_create` asks `rlimit_nproc_ok()` and refuses the fork past the cap. Root keeps a reserve (CAP_RESOURCE) so an admin can always clean up.

security.what: break out of the VM into the host (concept: UzOS is the guest)
security.story: Break out of the virtual machine into the host, usually through a bug in an emulated device or instruction. UzOS runs **as the guest** under QEMU, so an escape would mean attacking QEMU itself - a real exploit, out of scope for a teaching OS. Nothing is launched.

defence.fix: concept: the host walls off the guest; escape is a host-side exploit
defence.called: nothing in UzOS: the boundary is enforced by the HOST (QEMU/KVM), not by the guest. UzOS is the guest and cannot, and should not, implement an escape.
defence.why: honesty - writing a working QEMU escape would be a real exploit, out of scope for a teaching OS. This documents the boundary and where it is kept.
defence.story: The boundary is kept by the host: hypervisor patches, least privilege for the VM process, and strict device models. A guest cannot and should not implement its own escape.

security.what: a loop that never returns and never yields the CPU
security.story: `while (1);` makes no progress but never gives the CPU back.

defence.fix: no progress test is impossible; a CPU-time budget stops the spin
defence.called: the timer tick, through rlimit_check_cpu() (core/rlimit).
defence.why: `while (1);` by mistake would otherwise freeze that process (and, at a high priority, the machine) until a reboot.
defence.story: A kernel cannot tell a stuck loop from useful work, so the "watchdog" is a CPU-time budget: the timer tick (`rlimit_check_cpu`) kills a process that runs past its RLIMIT_CPU. Same machinery as cpu_exhaustion, different lesson: you do not detect "stuck", you bound how long anything may run.

security.what: read kernel memory from ring 3 via speculation (illustration)
security.story: Meltdown reads a kernel byte the page tables forbid, in the window before the CPU raises the fault, and leaks it through cache timing. It needs a specific out-of-order CPU; UzOS is a simple 32-bit kernel and **cannot run a real Meltdown**. We illustrate the line it attacks, not a working exploit.

defence.fix: kernel pages lack the user bit; ring 3 faults if it reads them
defence.called: the CPU, on every memory access, using the PAGE_USER bit UzOS sets when it maps memory (core/vmm map, core/umem for ring 3).
defence.why: the architectural line "ring 3 may not read kernel memory" is the U/S bit. UzOS is a simple 32-bit kernel and cannot run a real Meltdown; the defence shown here is that very line, which real mitigations (KPTI, microcode) exist to keep unbroken.
defence.story: A kernel page is present but has no PAGE_USER bit, so a ring 3 read faults. The CPU enforces this on every access; UzOS sets the bit when it maps memory (core/vmm, core/umem). Real systems keep this line with KPTI and microcode; here the lesson is the U/S bit itself.

security.what: ring 3 asks for nice 1000 / -20, renices others, or SCHED_FIFO 99
security.story: `setpriority(which, who, nice)` and `sched_setscheduler(pid, policy, param)` take **every** number from the caller. The ring 3 program [priority_out_of_range.s](priority_out_of_range.s) runs as user 1 and asks for six things it should not get.

modes.text: lists the five calls and what each would do
runs the program in ring 3; all six calls should come back refused (-1)

security.tryIt:
seclab attack priority_out_of_range live
audit

defence.fix: nice -20..19, rt 1..99; users only nicer, real-time needs RLIMIT_RTPRIO
defence.called: priority_set_nice() (core/priority) and policy_set() (core/policy), used by setpriority, sched_setscheduler, sched_setparam, sched_setattr and the commands nice, renice, chrt, before anything is changed.
defence.why: the numbers come from a user program. nice 1000 / rt 1000   rank above everything, forever nice -20 by a user    jumps ahead of every other user SCHED_FIFO by a user  a busy loop that only throttling stops And a user who renices the shell slows it for everybody.

security.what: a user takes root-only scheduler rights with legal-looking calls
security.story: Take an action only a more privileged user should: lower your nice below your budget, or make yourself real-time, and you outrank everyone. The numbers are legal; a user just is not allowed to use them.

defence.fix: every privileged CPU action checks uid and caps; no path skips it
defence.called: setpriority / sched_setscheduler / sched_setattr (cpu_management/syscalls), through def_nice_change_allowed and def_policy_change_allowed (security/priority_abuse). The uid to cap for comes from caps_of() (security/caps).
defence.why: priority_abuse feeds BAD NUMBERS; this is the other half - IN-RANGE actions a user simply is not allowed to take.
defence.story: Every privileged CPU syscall (`setpriority`, `sched_setscheduler`, `sched_setattr`) checks the caller's uid and caps through `def_nice_change_allowed` / `def_policy_change_allowed` (security/priority_abuse). A user gets only what its rlimits allow; root (CAP_PRIORITY) gets the rest. This is the partner of priority_abuse: that one sends bad numbers, this one sends legal numbers a user may not use.

security.what: a SCHED_FIFO busy loop outranks everything and never yields
security.story: A SCHED_FIFO task runs before every normal task and need never yield, so a real-time busy loop would own the CPU for good.

defence.fix: real-time tasks get at most 95% of each second; the rest is fair
defence.called: the scheduler tick (priority_tick, core/priority); the live count is priority_rt_throttle_count(). The right to BECOME real-time is a separate gate (def_policy_change_allowed).
defence.why: a real-time task runs before every normal one and need never sleep; without a throttle it would freeze the machine for good.
defence.story: Two gates. You need RLIMIT_RTPRIO to become real-time at all (see policy_restriction). Even then, the scheduler caps all real-time work at 95% of each second (`priority_tick`); past the budget it runs normal tasks, so the shell survives.

security.what: seize every slot, descriptor or byte, not just the CPU
security.story: Grab every finite resource - process slots, file descriptors, heap - not only CPU time.

defence.fix: CPU, procs, files, file size and heap each carry a per-process cap
defence.called: each limit is enforced at the place the resource is used - RLIMIT_CPU in the timer, NPROC in process_create, NOFILE in open(), FSIZE in write(), DATA in sbrk() (all core/rlimit).
defence.why: without limits one process can take every slot, every file descriptor or all of memory and leave nothing for the rest.
defence.story: Each resource carries a per-process limit (rlimit), checked where it is handed out: CPU in the timer, NPROC in `process_create`, NOFILE in `open`, FSIZE in `write`, DATA in `sbrk`. A child inherits the limits, so one quota covers a whole process tree.

security.what: chain existing code gadgets via stacked returns (concept)
security.story: Overflow a stack with a list of return addresses, each pointing at a short tail of existing code (a "gadget") ending in `ret`. The CPU runs gadget after gadget - a new program built from old code, injecting nothing.

defence.fix: concept: W^X/ASLR/CFI stop ROP; UzOS 32-bit paging has no NX bit
defence.called: nothing new: W^X and the no-execute bit are CPU features UzOS does not have (32-bit paging without PAE has no NX bit), and ASLR/CFI are build-time choices. This reports the honest gap.
defence.why: honesty - UzOS's page model has PAGE_WRITABLE and PAGE_USER but no execute bit, so it cannot enforce W^X. The lesson is what the defences are and why this kernel cannot run them.
defence.story: W^X (no page both writable and executable), ASLR (unpredictable addresses) and CFI (returns must land on real call sites). **UzOS cannot enforce W^X**: 32-bit paging without PAE has no no-execute bit. This pair teaches the defences and is honest that this kernel's page model (`PAGE_WRITABLE`, `PAGE_USER`, no NX) cannot run them.

security.what: flip a neighbour row's bits by hammering DRAM (concept)
security.story: Hammer one DRAM row thousands of times until the disturbance flips a bit in a neighbouring row - memory you were never allowed to write. It is a physical property of real DRAM.

defence.fix: concept: emulated RAM cannot flip bits; ECC/refresh fix real DRAM
defence.called: nothing in UzOS: emulated memory does not leak charge, and the real fixes live in the memory controller (ECC, refresh, Target Row Refresh), not in the operating system.
defence.why: honesty - Rowhammer needs physical DRAM; QEMU cannot reproduce it, so there is nothing for the OS to enforce.
defence.story: ECC memory, higher refresh rates and Target Row Refresh, all in the memory controller - not the OS. UzOS runs on emulated memory that cannot flip bits, so there is nothing to reproduce or enforce here.

security.what: switch your own policy to real-time to jump ahead of everyone
security.story: Set your own policy to SCHED_FIFO and you run before every normal process - jumping the queue with no busy loop.

defence.fix: a user may not switch to a real-time policy without RLIMIT_RTPRIO
defence.called: sched_setscheduler / sched_setattr (cpu_management/syscalls), through def_policy_change_allowed (security/priority_abuse).
defence.why: picking your own policy (say SCHED_FIFO) is a way to jump the queue ahead of everyone. The gate decides who is allowed to.
defence.story: `sched_setscheduler`/`sched_setattr` ask `def_policy_change_allowed` (security/priority_abuse): a user may pick a normal policy for its own process, but a real-time one only with RLIMIT_RTPRIO, and never for a system process. Root may do anything in range.

security.what: ring 3 reads the cycle counter to time the kernel (side channel)
security.story: The kernel does more work in some cases than in others. Looking up a file that exists walks further through the directory than looking up one that does not.

modes.text: the kernel (ring 0, where rdtsc is allowed) times both lookups and shows the gap
runs the program as user 1; with the defence it is killed at its first rdtsc ([CPU FAULT] #13 ... rdtsc)

security.tryIt:
seclab attack tsc_timing
seclab attack tsc_timing live
faults

defence.fix: set CR4.TSD: rdtsc in ring 3 faults, so programs get only a coarse clock
defence.called: tsc_init() (core/tsc) switches it on at boot; fault_handler() (core/faults) reports each refused rdtsc.
defence.why: a clock that counts single cycles is the first tool of a TIMING ATTACK. If the kernel takes a little longer for "file exists" than for "no such file", or for one key bit than for another, a program with rdtsc can see the difference and learn what it was never told. Programs still have uptime(), which moves in 10 ms steps: far too coarse for that. (Linux keeps rdtsc open for speed; seccomp can close it. Here we choose the safe side to show the switch.)

security.what: leak a value across a speculatively-crossed boundary (illustration)
security.story: Spectre makes the CPU execute past a check speculatively, reads a forbidden value in that window, and leaks it by cache timing. It needs branch prediction and out-of-order execution to train and measure; UzOS has neither, so it **cannot run a real Spectre**.

defence.fix: kernel memory has no user bit; speculation cannot cross the line
defence.called: the CPU, on every access, via the PAGE_USER bit (core/vmm, core/umem). Real Spectre mitigation also needs microcode and speculation barriers the hardware provides.
defence.why: UzOS cannot train a branch predictor or run a real Spectre; the lesson is that isolation is the boundary being attacked.
defence.story: Kernel memory is mapped without the user bit, so neither a normal nor a speculative ring 3 access may read it - the boundary Spectre tries to cross. Real mitigations add microcode and speculation barriers on top of this architectural line.

security.what: a busy loop at priority 7 starves every process below it
security.story: With **strict** priorities the scheduler always picks the highest READY process. A process at level 7 that never sleeps is always READY, so.

modes.text: the arithmetic: how long the victim and the shell wait with aging
starts hog at 7 and victim at 1 (counts its turns), sleeps the shell for 1 s, then reports who got the CPU; the hog is killed before printing

security.tryIt:
seclab attack cpu_hog
seclab attack cpu_hog live

defence.fix: a READY process rises one level per 100 ms of waiting: no starvation
defence.called: priority_effective() (core/priority), for every candidate on every scheduling decision; priority_pick_next() reports rescues.
defence.why: with strict priorities, one busy loop at level 7 keeps every lower process off the CPU forever, the shell included: the OS looks frozen. With aging, a process at level 1 climbs one level every 100 ms; after 600 ms it ties the hog and the round robin gives it a turn. Nobody waits forever.

security.what: ring 3 runs div 0, ud2, cli, in, hlt: each is a CPU exception
security.story: Five tiny ring 3 programs ([user_exception.s](user_exception.s)), each running one instruction the CPU refuses.

modes.text: lists the programs and the exception each one raises
runs all five as user 1 in ring 3; each is killed with a [CPU FAULT] report, the shell keeps working

security.tryIt:
seclab attack user_exception live
faults

defence.fix: a CPU exception in ring 3 kills that process, not the whole OS
defence.called: every CPU exception handler: fault_handler() (core/faults) and the page fault handler (memory_management/core/vmm).
defence.rules:
1. the fault came from ring 3 (low 2 bits of the saved CS = 3)
2. it is not one of the "machine is broken" exceptions:
2 NMI, 8 double fault, 18 machine check
Both true -> kill the process. Otherwise -> halt the kernel.
defence.why: without a handler, every exception ended in "System Halted!". Then any user program could stop the whole OS with one `div` by zero or one `cli`. A ring 3 fault only proves that THIS program is broken; the kernel's own data is untouched. A ring 0 fault proves the kernel is broken: going on could corrupt everything, so stopping is the safe choice.

security.what: an out-of-range video resolution to overflow framebuffer math
security.story: `bga_set_video_mode(w, h, bpp)` switches the graphics card's mode. Other code sizes the framebuffer as `w * h * bpp/8`. A mode like 65535x65535x32 overflows that math; a zero width makes a zero-size buffer. Later draws then run off the end.

defence.fix: a video mode must fit the card's size and be a real colour depth
defence.called: bga_set_video_mode() (gui/bga/bga.c), before it programs the card registers.
defence.why: other code sizes the framebuffer as width * height * bpp/8 and maps/draws it. A huge or zero mode would overflow that math or make a zero-size buffer, and later draws would run off its end.
defence.story: `bga_set_video_mode()` now asks `def_bga_mode_ok` first: width/height must be non-zero and within the card's maximum, and bpp a real depth (15/16/24/32). This check did not exist before — the attack is what revealed the gap.

security.what: drawing with negative or huge coordinates writes outside the pixel buffer
security.story: Pixel `(x, y)` is stored at `pixels[y * width + x]`. If `x` or `y` is negative, or a shape runs past the right or bottom edge, that index points **outside** the buffer, into whatever the heap put next to it. The old window manager's text drawing checked only the right and bottom edges, so text at a negative `x` wrote in front of the window's buffer.

modes.text: shows the index the old code computed for x = -8

allocates a 16 × 16 canvas with 64 guard words (0xDEADBEEF) on each side, draws 5 shapes hanging over every edge (including one where x + w overflows a 32-bit int), and counts damaged guard words. Then frees it.

security.tryIt: seclab attack canvas_overflow live

defence.fix: cut every rectangle to the canvas before drawing
defence.called: canvas_fill_rect() and canvas_blit() (gui/canvas), before any pixel is written.
defence.why: pixel (x, y) lives at pixels[y * width + x]. With x = -8 that is 8 pixels BEFORE the row, which for row 0 is before the whole buffer: the heap block in front gets overwritten. Windows dragged half off-screen do this all the time, so clipping is normal and is NOT logged.

security.what: install colours that hide text by matching the background
security.story: It installs a colour theme that hides text. Text cells only store a colour **number**; the theme decides what that number looks like. Make colour 15 ("white") the same as the background and every message printed in white is still on screen, but unreadable.

modes.text: explains the trick
calls the real palette_use() with both themes; both must be refused and the current theme must stay

security.tryIt:
seclab attack invisible_text live
theme                             # still the theme you had

defence.fix: refuse text colours that are invisible on their background
defence.called: palette_use() (vga/palette) for every theme, and the shell's `color` command, before the colours are used.
defence.why: text in the same colour as its background is still there, but nobody can see it. An attacker can hide output that way: a warning, a "kill" that happened, or a fake prompt the user types a password into. The screen must never lie by omission.

security.what: open IRQ lines that no driver handles, inviting an interrupt storm
security.story: The PIC has 16 IRQ lines; a **mask** bit per line decides whether the CPU hears it. The old `pic_remap()` opened all 16. A device on a line with no driver, like a serial port picking up noise, raises its line and nobody ever answers the device. The CPU is interrupted, finds no handler, sends EOI, and is interrupted again: an **interrupt storm**.

modes.text: lists every open line and flags any without a handler
tries pic_unmask() on IRQ 3, 4, 5 and 7 (serial, sound, printer: no drivers), then checks the PIC mask did not change

security.tryIt:
seclab attack irq_storm
seclab attack irq_storm live
devices

defence.fix: keep every IRQ line masked until a driver handles it
defence.called: pic_unmask() (pic/), before a line is opened.
defence.why: an open line with no driver can still fire. Nobody reads the device, so it keeps asking: each time the CPU stops, finds no handler, sends EOI, and gets interrupted again. A noisy or broken device can keep the CPU busy forever (an "interrupt storm"). Lines are closed until a driver is ready for them.

security.what: type faster than the shell reads to overrun the key buffer
security.story: The keyboard IRQ adds a key per press; the shell reads them later. Type faster than they are read and an unbounded buffer would overrun into kernel memory.

defence.fix: the key ring buffer drops input when full; it never overruns
defence.called: enqueue() (keyboard/keyboard.c), for every key the IRQ adds.
defence.why: the keyboard interrupt fires faster than the shell reads. A fixed ring buffer that drops when full can never overrun into kernel memory, however fast keys arrive. (No audit log here: this runs in the interrupt, where logging is unsafe.)
defence.story: `enqueue()` in `keyboard.c` asks `def_key_queue_has_room()` before storing a key; a full ring buffer drops the newest key instead of overwriting. Keystrokes can be lost under a flood, but memory is never corrupted. (No audit log: this runs in the interrupt, where logging is unsafe — the verdict comes from the selftest.)

security.what: big mouse movements push the pointer outside the screen
security.story: A PS/2 mouse never says where it is, only how far it moved (at most 255 per packet). The driver keeps a running sum. Pushing left at `x = 0` makes the sum negative; the GUI then uses it as a pixel index and draws outside the screen buffer.

modes.text: shows where 10 big moves left would end without a check
feeds 10 × 255 moves in each of the 4 directions to the **real** packet decoder (interrupts off), prints the pointer after each, then puts it back

security.tryIt: seclab attack mouse_coordinate_escape live

defence.fix: clamp the mouse pointer to the screen after every move
defence.called: the mouse packet decoder (mouse/), for every new x and y, and mouse_set_screen() when the screen size changes.
defence.why: the pointer position is used as a pixel index when the GUI draws it and checks clicks. Moving left from x = 0 would give a negative index: writes before the screen buffer. Hitting the edge is normal, so clamping is NOT logged.

security.what: one stray byte shifts every following mouse packet
security.story: A mouse packet is 3 bytes, but nothing in the stream marks where a packet starts. The old decoder just counted 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2 ... One lost or extra byte, for example when a key press and a mouse move race on the shared PS/2 controller, puts it one byte out of step for good.

modes.text: shows how a naive decoder misreads the bytes

with interrupts off, feeds the **real** decoder a stray byte, then "left click + move right 10", then a packet with the overflow bit set. Checks the click and move came out right and the overflow was dropped. Puts the pointer back.

security.tryIt:
seclab attack mouse_desync live
audit

defence.fix: resync on bit 3 of the first byte; drop overflowed packets
defence.called: the mouse packet decoder (mouse/).
defence.rules:
1. a packet's first byte always has bit 3 set; if a byte at
the start of a packet doesn't, drop it and wait
2. a packet whose overflow bits (6, 7) are set is dropped
defence.why: the mouse sends a stream of bytes with no markers. If one byte is lost (or an extra one arrives), every later packet is read shifted by one: movements become button presses and the pointer jumps around. Bit 3 is the only "this is the start" sign the protocol has, so we use it to find our step again.

security.what: a missing or broken RTC returns impossible dates (month 165)
security.story: It plays a broken clock chip: register values that cannot be a date.

modes.text: shows what 0xFF decodes to and which table it would overrun
feeds all three register sets to rtc_decode(); each must be refused, then the real clock is read to show it still works

security.tryIt:
seclab attack rtc_garbage
seclab attack rtc_garbage live

defence.fix: refuse any date/time from the RTC that cannot exist
defence.called: rtc_decode() (rtc/), after decoding, before anyone sees the date.
defence.why: the RTC is hardware outside the kernel's control: a dead battery, a missing chip (every read gives 0xFF) or a broken emulator can return anything. Code after it trusts the date: rtc_month_name(month) indexes a table, rtc_unix_time() uses month - 1 as an index. Month 165 would read far past the table.

security.what: a 0 or out-of-range speaker frequency: divide by zero or noise
security.story: `speaker_on(hz)` programs the PIT with `1193180 / hz`. A 0 divides by zero (CPU exception); a very low hz overflows the 16-bit divisor; a huge hz is inaudible noise.

defence.fix: only play PC-speaker tones from 20 Hz to 20 kHz (never divide by 0)
defence.called: speaker_on() (speaker/speaker.c), before dividing or writing.
defence.why: speaker_on() computes divisor = 1193180 / hz and writes it to the PIT. hz = 0 divides by zero; hz below 20 gives a divisor that does not fit 16 bits; hz above 20 kHz is inaudible noise.
defence.story: `speaker_on()` asks `def_speaker_freq_ok` first and only lets 20 Hz..20 kHz reach the divide and the speaker port. Everything else is refused and logged.

security.what: start the timer at 0 Hz (divide by zero) or a rate the PIT cannot do
security.story: `init_timer(hz)` computes `divisor = 1193180 / hz` and writes it to the PIT's 16-bit counter.

modes.text: explains each bad rate
calls the real init_timer() with all three, then checks the timer still runs at 100 Hz

security.tryIt:
seclab attack timer_divide_by_zero live
uptime

defence.fix: only accept PIT rates whose divisor fits in 16 bits (never 0)
defence.called: init_timer() (timer/), before any division or port write.
defence.why: init_timer() computes divisor = 1193180 / hz. hz = 0      -> division by zero: CPU exception, kernel halts hz < 19     -> divisor > 65535: cut to 16 bits, wrong rate hz > 1.19 M -> divisor 0, which the PIT reads as 65536 A wrong tick rate breaks sleep(), uptime and scheduling.

security.what: open window after window until the slot table is full
security.story: Open window after window. The window manager has MAX_WINDOWS fixed slots, each with a heap canvas; without a cap a program takes them all and nothing else can open one.

defence.fix: refuse a new window once all MAX_WINDOWS slots are in use
defence.called: wm_create_window() (gui/wm/window_manager.c), before a slot is taken.
defence.why: the window table has MAX_WINDOWS fixed slots. Without a cap a program could ask for window after window until the table (and the heap behind each canvas) is exhausted and nothing else can open one.
defence.story: `wm_create_window()` asks `def_window_quota_ok` before taking a slot and refuses once all are in use. The attack opens MAX_WINDOWS + 4 tiny windows and sees the extras refused, then destroys the ones it made.

security.what: ask for a window so large that kmalloc(w*h*4) overflows
security.story: `wm_create_window` allocates its canvas with `kmalloc(w * h * 4)`. A size like 100000x100000 overflows that multiply (kmalloc returns a tiny buffer the first draw overruns) or drains the heap.

defence.fix: a window must be positive and no bigger than the screen
defence.called: wm_create_window() (gui/wm/window_manager.c), before it allocates the window's canvas.
defence.why: wm_create_window() does kmalloc(width * height * 4). A giant size overflows that multiplication (so kmalloc returns a tiny buffer that later draws overrun) or simply drains the heap.
defence.story: `wm_create_window()` now asks `def_window_size_ok` first: width/height must be positive and no bigger than the screen. Like bga_mode_overflow, this check did not exist before — the attack revealed the gap.

syscalls.summary: close(fd): the number becomes free for the next open().
syscalls.details:
Closing lowers the file's open count; once nobody has it open, it may
be deleted. Files a process forgets to close are closed for it when it
ends (fd_cleanup).

syscalls.summary: seek(fd, offset, whence): jump to another place in a file.
syscalls.details:

  seek(fd, -4, SEEK_END)   the last 4 bytes

The new position must be between 0 and the largest file size.
syscalls.uses: the fd table (core/fd), RAMDISK_MAX_FILE_SIZE (filesystem_management), and the defence descriptor_bounds.

security.what: a process ends without closing its files; they stay 'open' forever
security.story: Every open descriptor keeps its file's `open_count` up, and a file with a count above zero cannot be deleted. A process that **ends without `close()`** (it forgot, crashed, or was killed) leaves that count up forever. The file is stuck until reboot.

modes.text: explains the leak
creates /seclab_leak, starts a process that opens it and returns at once, waits for it to end and be reaped, then shows the open count and tries rm

security.tryIt:
seclab attack fd_leak live
audit                            # fd_cleanup closed the leaked file

defence.fix: close every file a process left open when it ends
defence.called: the reaper (process_management), just before a dead process's slot is freed.
defence.why: each open descriptor holds the file's open count up. A process that ends (or is killed) without close() would leave the count up forever, so busy_check would never let anyone delete that file. Programs forget, crash, or get killed: the kernel must clean up for them.

security.what: use descriptor numbers that are out of range, closed, or the wrong kind
security.story: A file descriptor is just a number the program hands to the kernel, which uses it as an index into the process's 16-entry `fd_table`.

modes.text: lists the bad uses
really makes each call (with a temporary read-only file for the last one), then deletes the file

security.tryIt: seclab attack invalid_descriptor live

defence.fix: only use descriptors that exist, are open, and allow the operation
defence.called: sys_read, sys_write, sys_close, sys_seek (syscalls/), first thing.
defence.rules:
1. 0 <= fd < MAX_FDS (it indexes the fd_table array)
2. stdin can only be read, stdout/stderr only written
3. a file descriptor must be open, and opened for what you do
(no write() on a file opened with O_READ only)
defence.why: fd is a number from the program. fd = -1 or 9999 indexes fd_table outside its 16 entries and reads a random pointer as a "file". A closed descriptor holds NULL.

security.what: read/write with a NULL, huge, or wrapping buffer
security.story: `read(fd, buf, count)` makes the kernel copy `count` bytes **into** `buf`; `write` copies **from** it. The program chooses both numbers.

modes.text: lists the bad buffers
really calls sys_read() / sys_write() with each, then a normal write that must still work

security.tryIt: seclab attack oversized_transfer live

defence.fix: refuse NULL, oversized or wrapping read/write buffers
defence.called: sys_read and sys_write (syscalls/), before any byte is copied.
defence.rules:
count == 0 is always fine (nothing to copy). Otherwise:
1. count <= IO_MAX_TRANSFER (16 KiB)
2. buf is not in the NULL page
3. buf + count does not wrap past 4 GiB
defence.why: read() copies 'count' bytes to 'buf'. A NULL buffer, a huge count, or a range that wraps around to address 0 makes that copy write over memory the caller never owned. (When the call comes from ring 3, the int 0x80 handler has already checked that the buffer is the caller's own memory.)

syscalls.name: getcwd
syscalls.summary: getcwd(buf, size): write the current directory's path.
syscalls.details:
The VFS only stores names and parent links, so the path is built by
walking up from the directory to the root.

syscalls.name: rename
syscalls.summary: rename(from, to): move or rename an entry.
syscalls.details:
rename("a", "b")        rename a to b in the same directory
  rename("a", "docs")     docs is a directory: move a into it, keep the name
  rename("a", "docs/b")   move into docs and call it b

Moving takes the entry out of its directory and puts it in another:
you must be allowed to remove it from the first (own it, write on the
directory) and to write into the second (core/perm).
syscalls.uses: vfs_lookup / vfs_lookup_parent (core/vfs), ramdisk_move (core/ramdisk), which checks the new name and refuses loops, perm_may_remove / perm_check (user_management).

security.what: names like '..', 'a/b' or 300 characters break paths or overflow buffers
security.story: Some names break the filesystem as soon as they exist.

modes.text: lists the names and their problems
really calls ramdisk_create() with each name in /, and vfs_lookup() with a 300-character component. Anything created by mistake is deleted again.

security.tryIt: seclab attack bad_filename live

defence.fix: bound every path component; refuse ., .., '/', spaces in new names
defence.called: vfs_lookup / vfs_lookup_parent (core/vfs) for every component, ramdisk_create / ramdisk_move (core/ramdisk) for new names.
defence.rules:
component - 1 to FS_NAME_MAX characters (fits the name buffer)
new name  - also: not "." or "..", no '/', only visible
characters (no spaces or control codes)
defence.why: a 200-character component copied into a 128-byte buffer overflows it. A file called ".." or "a/b" can never be reached by a path, and one with spaces cannot be typed in the shell.

security.what: delete a file or directory that is still in use: use after free
security.story: `rm` frees the node with `kfree()`. Three things can still point at it.

modes.text: lists the three cases
builds each case for real in / and calls sys_unlink(): an open file, a directory with a file in it, and the current directory. Then cleans up properly.

security.tryIt:
seclab attack delete_open_file live
ls                               # no seclab_* entries left

defence.fix: never delete an open file, a non-empty directory, or a current directory
defence.called: ramdisk_delete() (core/ramdisk), before anything is freed.
defence.rules:
a node may be deleted only if
1. no descriptor has it open        (open_count == 0)
2. it is not a directory with entries
3. it is not the root
4. no process has it as its current directory
defence.why: deleting frees the node's memory. A descriptor or a cwd still pointing at it would then use freed memory ("use after free"): the next kmalloc() reuses that memory for something else, and reading the "file" reads, or writes, that something else.

security.what: move a directory into its own subdirectory, making a loop

modes.text: draws the loop it would make
builds /seclab_a/b, tries to move seclab_a into b, and into itself as seclab_a/inner (both refused), then removes the directories

security.tryIt: seclab attack dir_cycle live

defence.fix: refuse to move a directory into itself or its own subdirectories
defence.called: ramdisk_move() (core/ramdisk), before anything is relinked.
defence.why: "mv /a /a/b/c" would make a's parent one of its own children. The whole subtree is cut off from the root (lost), and code that walks up to the root, like pwd, would go round forever.

security.what: a huge file offset wraps around and writes outside the file
security.story: A write gives an `offset` and a `size`. The obvious check adds them.

modes.text: shows the sum the naive check computes
creates a temporary file, tries the wrapping write and a write one byte past 64 KiB (both refused), a normal write (allowed), then deletes the file

security.tryIt: seclab attack file_offset_wrap live

defence.fix: check offset + size against the file limit without wrapping
defence.called: ramdisk_write() (core/ramdisk), before memory is grown or copied.
defence.why: the obvious check "offset + size <= limit" wraps in 32 bits: 0xFFFFFFF0 + 0x20 = 0x10, which passes, and the copy then writes 4 GiB past the file's buffer.

commands.name: chmod
commands.summary: who may read and write a file.
commands.details:
chmod 60 notes      only I may read and write it      rw/--
  chmod 64 notes      others may read it too            rw/r-
  chmod 40 notes      read-only, even for me            r-/--

Each digit is 4 (read) + 2 (write): the first is for the owner, the
second for everybody else. Only the owner and root may change it.
commands.uses: perm_parse / perm_may_chmod / perm_format (core/perm), vfs_lookup (filesystem_management), arg_next (lib), ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: chown
commands.summary: give a file to another user.
commands.details:
chown guest /home/guest/notes

Needs CAP_CHOWN (root). (If anyone could give files away, a user could hand a
file to someone else and make them look responsible for it, or slip
past that user's limits. Linux has the same rule.)
commands.uses: users_find_name (core/users), caps_require (security_management), vfs_lookup (filesystem_management), arg_next (lib), ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: id
commands.summary: a user's uid, name and home directory.
commands.details:
id          you:   uid=1(guest) home=/home/guest
id root     root:  uid=0(root)  home=/home/root  (the administrator)
commands.uses: users_find_* (core/users), process_caller_uid (process_management), ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: logout
commands.summary: end the session, back to the login prompt.
commands.details:
Like a terminal that closes, logout "hangs up" the session: every job
the shell started gets SIGHUP and ends, unless it was started with
`nohup` (or `setsid`, which puts it in a session of its own).
commands.uses: session_login_prompt (core/session), vga_clear (device_management), process_hangup (process_management core/process), ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: passwd
commands.summary: change a password.
commands.details:
passwd          your own: type the old one first, then the new one twice
passwd guest    CAP_USERS (root) only: set guest's password (no old one needed)
commands.uses: users_* (core/users), session_* (core/session), caps_* (security_management), ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: su
commands.summary: become another user ("switch user").
commands.details:
su          become root
  su guest    become guest

You must type that user's password, except when you hold CAP_SETUID
(root): root may become anyone. Afterwards the shell runs with the new uid and
starts in the new user's home. `logout` ends the session.
commands.uses: users_find_name (core/users), session_* (core/session), caps_caller_has (security_management), ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: useradd
commands.summary: create a new account (CAP_USERS: root).
commands.details:
useradd alice      asks for alice's password twice, then:
                     uid 1000, home /home/alice (owned by alice)

Names are 1-15 characters: "a"-"z", "0"-"9", "_", starting with a
letter. Each new user gets the next uid; uids are never reused.
commands.uses: users_add / users_name_ok (core/users), session_ask_new_password (core/session), caps_require (security_management), ui_*.

commands.name: userdel
commands.summary: remove an account (CAP_USERS: root).
commands.details:
Refused for root, for the user you are, and for a user who still has
processes running (kill them first). The home directory and files
stay; `ls` then shows their owner as "#1000": the uid of a user who no
longer exists. That uid is never given to anyone else.
commands.uses: users_find_name / users_delete (core/users), session_user (core/session), the process table (process_management), caps_require (security_management), ui_*.

commands.name: users
commands.summary: every account in the user table.
commands.details:
┌─ Users ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   UID  NAME         HOME           PROCS  HASH        │
  │     0  root         /home/root         3  4f1c09a2... │

HASH is the start of the stored password hash. The passwords
themselves are not stored anywhere, so they cannot be shown.
commands.uses: users_slot (core/users), the process table (process_management), box_* / ui_* (ui module).

commands.name: whoami
commands.summary: the name of the user this shell runs as.
commands.details: The shell is a process like any other; its uid is "who you are".
commands.uses: process_caller_uid (process_management), users_name (core/users).

syscalls.name: getuid
syscalls.summary: the uid of the calling process.

syscalls.name: setuid
syscalls.summary: change the caller's uid.
syscalls.details:
Root uses this to give up its rights: a program started by root can
switch to a normal user before it does risky work. Nobody may use it
to GET more rights; the defence setuid_guard decides.

security.what: a guest program reads, overwrites and deletes root's files
security.story: As root, the attack makes two files: `/home/root/secret` (mode 60) and `/seclab_root_file` (mode 64). Then the ring 3 program [file_permission_bypass.s](file_permission_bypass.s) runs as guest and tries four syscalls.

modes.text: lists the four tries
runs them; every one should say denied

security.tryIt:
su
seclab attack file_permission_bypass live
seclab repair

defence.fix: files are used only as their owner and mode allow; root passes
defence.called: perm_check / perm_may_remove / perm_may_chmod (core/perm), which sys_open, sys_mkdir, sys_unlink, sys_rename, sys_chdir, `ls`, `chmod` and the ELF loader call before touching a file.
defence.rules:
1. CAP_FILES (root) may do anything
2. the owner gets the FIRST digit of the mode
3. everybody else gets the SECOND digit
4. the wanted bits (4 = read, 2 = write) must all be there
Removing a file or changing its mode: owner or CAP_FILES only.
defence.why: without this, every user can read every other user's files, overwrite them, or delete them: users would have names but nothing of their own.

security.what: a guest program in ring 3 calls setuid(0) to become root
security.story: The ring 3 program [setuid_escalation.s](setuid_escalation.s) runs as guest (uid 1), calls `setuid(0)`, then `getuid()` (who am I now?) and `getcaps()` (which privileges do I have now?), and leaves the answers in the usertask mailbox.

modes.text: explains what uid 0 would give the program
runs it; expected: setuid(0) returned -1, getuid() is now 1 and getcaps() = 0x0

security.tryIt:
su
seclab attack setuid_escalation live

defence.fix: only root may change its uid; nobody can make itself root
defence.called: sys_setuid() (syscalls/setuid), before the uid is changed.
defence.rules:
1. the wanted uid belongs to a real user
2. CAP_SETUID (root) may become any user
3. anyone else may only "become" itself (nothing changes)
defence.why: the uid is the ONE number every other check trusts: kill_guard, priority_bounds, file permissions. If a program could set its own uid to 0, every one of those checks would wave it through.

commands.name: audit
commands.summary: what the defences refused, and to whom.
commands.details:
audit        the newest events, newest first:

                41.27s  guest   PID 2     kill_guard
                                          kill refused: not yours

audit sum    how often each defence refused since boot, and how
             many of those audit_limit only counted (a flood). These
             counters never forget, even when the ring is full.
commands.uses: audit_snapshot / audit_source (core/audit), users_find_uid (user_management), timer_frequency (device_management), arg_next (lib/args), ui_* / ui_cell (ui module).

commands.name: caps
commands.summary: which privileges a user holds.
commands.details:
caps          you
  caps root     root

  > Capabilities of guest (uid 1)
    x CAP_KILL       stop processes of other users
    x CAP_SETUID     become another user, no password
    ...

Every privileged check in the kernel asks for one of these (core/caps).
commands.uses: caps_* (core/caps), users_find_* (user_management), process_caller_uid (process_management), ui_* / ui_cell (ui).

commands.name: integrity
commands.summary: is the kernel still the one that booted?
commands.details:
> Kernel integrity
    REGION     SECTION  SIZE     AT BOOT    NOW
    code       .text    170 KB   4f1c09a2   4f1c09a2  unchanged
    constants  .rodata   25 KB   9be0712c   9be0712c  unchanged

Shows the first 4 bytes of each SHA-256; they are compared in full.
commands.uses: integrity_* (core/integrity), tsc_* (cpu_management) to time the check, ui_* / ui_cell (ui module).

commands.name: seclab
commands.summary: explore the attacks and defences.
commands.details:
seclab list                  every attack and its defence
  seclab info <attack>         what it does and what stops it
  seclab attack <id>           simulate: read-only, always safe
  seclab attack <id> live      really run it (small, bounded; CAP_SECLAB)
  seclab defence <id>          show a defence (by its id or its attack's)
  seclab verify <id> | all     run defence selftests
  seclab log                   newest refusals first (the same as `audit`)
  seclab status                counters, watchdog, free process slots
  seclab repair                let every attack undo itself (CAP_SECLAB)

A live run is BLOCKED when the attack's OWN defence refused something
during it. Other defences may refuse too (an attack can trip several),
but only its own defence proves that this defence works.
commands.uses: registry, audit, watchdog and caps (core/), the process table for `status` and the reaper for `repair` (process_management), arg_next (lib/args), ui_* (ui module).

syscalls.name: getcaps
syscalls.summary: the capabilities of the calling process.

security.what: write one byte into the kernel's own code, then run a program
security.story: Code in ring 0 can write anywhere, also into the kernel's own instructions. UzOS maps its code writable, and `exec` programs run in ring 0, so a malicious program could do it. One byte is enough.

modes.text: shows the target's address and byte, and measures the kernel
1. patches the byte  2. starts /hello the way exec does  3. puts the byte back

security.tryIt:
su
integrity
seclab attack kernel_patch live
audit

defence.fix: hash kernel code at boot; refuse to run programs once it changed
defence.called: integrity_verify() (core/integrity), which elf_load_and_run() calls before it starts a program, and the `integrity` command.
defence.rules:
1. a region was measured at boot (its hash is not all zero)
2. its hash now is the same as at boot, byte for byte
A changed kernel starts no more programs until it is rebooted.
defence.why: code in ring 0 can write anywhere, also into the kernel's own instructions: one byte turns `if (!allowed) return 0;` into "always allowed". Every other defence trusts that the code it is made of is still the code that was built.

security.what: push a refusal out of the audit log with a flood of cheap ones
security.story: The audit ring keeps the newest 32 events. Whoever wants a refusal forgotten does not need to delete it: they only need 32 newer ones.

modes.text: explains how many events it takes
does steps 1-2 for real, then searches the ring for event #57 by its sequence number

security.tryIt:
su
seclab attack log_flood live
audit
audit sum

defence.fix: at most 10 events per defence per second in the ring; the rest are counted
defence.called: audit_log() (core/audit), for every event, before it is put into the ring.
defence.rules:
1. each defence may put AUDIT_BURST events into the ring per
second (AUDIT_WINDOW_TICKS)
2. after that, its events are still COUNTED, only not kept
3. a new second starts a new allowance
defence.why: the ring keeps the newest 32 events. Anyone who can make the kernel refuse something cheap, like close(-1), can push the one event that mattered out of it. With the limit, a flood fills at most 10 slots a second, and the counters (`audit sum`) still show every refusal. Linux does the same in its log (printk_ratelimit) and audit system (rate_limit).

commands.name: snake
commands.summary: the classic game, in text mode.
commands.details:
The board is a grid of cells (empty, wall, snake, food). The snake is
an array of positions, head first. Every game tick the head moves one
cell; the tail follows unless the snake just ate.

  arrows / WASD  turn        P / Space  pause
  R              restart     Q / Ctrl+C quit (the old screen comes back)

The game borrows the whole screen (vga_fullscreen) and centres the
board, so it works in every display mode.

security.what: calc input that divides by zero or overflows halts the kernel
security.story: `calc` runs inside the kernel. Some inputs make the CPU's divide instruction fault, and a fault in the kernel halts everything.

modes.text: lists the inputs and their effect
runs each through the real calc_eval(), then (2 + 3) * 4, which must still give 20

security.tryIt:
seclab attack calc_overflow live
calc -2147483648 / -1

defence.fix: check every calc step: fits 32 bits, no /0, no INT_MIN / -1
defence.called: calc_eval() (commands/calc), after every number and operation.
defence.rules:
1. every value and result fits a 32-bit int
2. never divide by 0
3. never divide INT_MIN by -1
defence.why: on x86, a 32-bit division by 0, AND -2147483648 / -1 (the answer +2147483648 does not fit), raise CPU exception 0. In the kernel that halts the whole OS. And silent overflow gives wrong answers: 2147483647 + 1 would print -2147483648. calc works in 64 bits and checks each step against these rules.

security.what: typing more characters than the line buffer holds
security.story: The line you type into is a fixed array of 256 bytes. Holding a key down sends hundreds of characters. Without a check, character 257 is written **after** the array, over the next variable in memory. That is the classic *buffer overflow*.

modes.text: explains the overflow
builds a test line with 16 guard words (0xDEADBEEF) right behind it, sends 1000 keys through the real line_insert(), then checks: 255 stored, NUL at the end, guards intact

security.tryIt: seclab attack line_overflow live

defence.fix: never store more typed characters than the line buffer holds
defence.called: line_insert() (core/line), before each character is stored.
defence.why: the line is a fixed array of 256 bytes. Storing the 257th character writes past the end, into whatever sits next to it in memory: the classic "buffer overflow", the bug behind many famous attacks. Keyboards can type forever; arrays cannot.

security.story: It starts a process whose **name** contains a newline and a fake row.

modes.text: shows how the raw name would print
starts a real process with that name, runs the real ps, then stops the process

security.tryIt: seclab attack output_spoof live

defence.fix: show names in tables cleaned (no control characters) and cut to fit
defence.called: ui_cell() (core/box), which tables use for every name they did not write themselves: process names in ps/top, and more.
defence.why: a table trusts that each cell is one short piece of text. A process named "x\n  1  kernel_main  RUNNING" would print a NEW line that looks exactly like a real process: the table now lies. A very long name pushes the next columns out of place. Cutting is normal (not logged); a control character in a name is never normal, so that is logged.
